speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON REPORTED RESTRICTION IN ADVERTISEMENT FOR ELECTRICAL MAINTENANCE MAN
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) inquired regarding an application for the position of electrical maintenance man at the Ottawa airport, which had been advertised by the civil service commission as open to residents of the Toronto air services region.
For purposes of efficient administration the air services branch of the Department of Transport operates through a series of regional headquarters which have extensive operational authority delegated to them. It is the custom of the civil service commission to advertise public competitions on an area basis related to these regional areas of administration.
The Ottawa river forms the boundary line between the Ontario and Quebec regions, so that the competition advertised for Ottawa airport through the Toronto headquarters would include the Ottawa area but not Hull. On the other hand, residents of Hull would be eligible for regional competitions in the Quebec area, which has its headquarters at Montreal.
This regional organization of our air services branch, including the present boundaries, and the civil service commission practice of advertising competitions on this regional basis, were established over 10 years ago under the previous administration. I am a little surprised, therefore, if the hon. member takes exception to the practice we are following, that he did not take the matter up with my predecessors under the previous government when they were in office.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of National Defence. Has the minister any statement to make to this house following his meeting in Paris with the other defence ministers?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON PARIS MEETING OF DEFENCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
I could make a brief statement if required, Mr. Speaker, as I expected there might be such a question raised.
I think the best way of describing this meeting would be to say it was a "technical session" during which were discussed various matters of interest to defence which will be further considered by the military committee in order that they may be brought forward to the NATO council in permanent session.
The question of the logistic support of the alliance was discussed with special reference to the problems of the Federal Republic of Germany. These are to be examined by the NATO military authorities in full co-operation with West Germany and the other nations directly concerned, which means that General Norstad will consider what contributions the various NATO countries can make to the solution of Germany's problems. It was urged that these be found within the NATO area.
Ministers also discussed ways in which the efforts of the alliance could be better coordinated in the fields of research, development and production in order to take advantage of the skills and capabilities available in NATO countries. This matter was referred to the NATO armaments committee. A list of various projects planned or under development in the several NATO countries will be submitted for study. In this way it is hoped to make progress toward preventing duplication. This item is of special interest to Canada. I expect that several of our country's projects will be reported upon and, of course, Canada would benefit if it were found that any were generally acceptable for use within the alliance.
Questions of defence planning were raised, increased emphasis being placed on immediate readiness and the first phase of a war. The military committee is to examine the suggestions made during the discussion and report by July 1 upon the consequences, particularly with respect to the logistics. As to sharing the burden, numerous suggestions were advanced so as to enable all member nations to train and maintain their forces at the level agreed upon by the north Atlantic council.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, April 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Regier.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last Thursday night I listened very attentively to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). First he gave us a resume of the economy, in which he could see nothing but roses.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I suggest that the hon. member wait for one minute, as there is considerable movement in the house at the moment which will soon settle down.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just saying, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance last Thursday night gave us a resume of the economy in which he could see nothing but roses. Then he proceeded to enumerate small changes described in various terms such as "minor" and "technical". For all practical purposes the budget did not create the spontaneous, resounding applause that those on the government side of the house had hoped for, because the position is practically the same as it was before March 31. No one anticipated a general slashing of taxes, but there was plenty of justification for anticipating the removal or at least a reduction of some taxes, such as the excise tax on passenger motor cars, which has been suffocating an industry that has contributed more to the coffers of the receiver general, to employment and to the all-round standard of living of Canadians than any other industry.
The automotive industry in Canada today can be regarded, directly and indirectly, as one of the major employers of labour. This industry provides more jobs than any other industry. The total value of its products in 1959 was $1 billion. There are approximately five million motor cars and trucks using the highways of this nation, and where great distances might seem an obstacle to national advancement the motor vehicle has supplemented the railways and the waterways in opening new territories for development.
I shall proceed to outline briefly the impact of the automotive industry on our national life. The reason I am bringing this

The Budget-Mr. Badanai industry to the attention of the Minister of Finance is that, nothwithstanding its many contributions, the minister has again ignored the need for the elimination of the discriminatory excise tax on automobiles which now, more than ever, is an obnoxious tax on Canadian made cars and is only creating a favourable climate for the sale of foreign importations.
There is no Canadian employment in the manufacture of imported passenger cars and substantially less tax revenue for the government from their sale, but the most important factor is the reduction in employment in the Canadian manufacturing plants. To illustrate this point, among the principal Canadian automobile factories the monthly average of employment was 40,243 in 1956, whereas in 1959 the monthly average of persons employed in these plants was only 33,160. Yet more passenger cars were sold in Canada last year than in 1956.
The hon. member for Laval, speaking on this subject last night, had this to say as found in the translation of his speech:
As you can see, this government has improved the economic situation of the country. In the field of industry, again there is progress. For the automobile industry, for instance, we have some revealing figures.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the revealing figures are the figures of new car registrations in Canada from 1955 to 1959 inclusive. These figures are as follows:

These figures are revealing indeed. They reveal the fact that if all these imported cars had been manufactured in Canada it would have resulted in the additional employment of roughly 16,400 persons. I am not suggesting

that the elimination of the excise tax would automatically stop the importation of automobiles, but I am sure it would result in a reduction in importations, and a beneficial effect on sales of Canadian made cars would undoubtedly be the outcome.
It is a matter of more than passing concern that the excise tax affects the share of the market obtained by Canadian companies. Even the most cursory examination of the share of the market obtained by the less expensive foreign cars leads to the conclusion that consumers are sensitive to variations in the price spread between imported and domestic models. The price spread resulting from the application of the excise tax on a Canadian produced car which is sold to the public for $3,000 and a European automobile which is sold for say $2,000 amounts to about $90. The removal of the excise tax and thus the removal of the price spread it creates of about $90 could have an important effect on the share of the market to be obtained by Canadian produced cars.
Relief from the excise tax on passenger cars is needed to help the Canadian motor car manufacturing industry combat the increasing sales of European cars, and would permit the continued growth of the Canadian passenger car manufacturing plants. But, Mr. Speaker, over and above all I have said with regard to the facts and figures, the excise tax is discriminatory because the automobile is the only major consumer article still subject to special taxation, and I submit to the minister that a re-examination of this provision should be made without undue delay looking to the elimination of this unwarranted tax.

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope he will correct me if I am wrong, but I understood him to say that if the excise tax on automobiles were removed it would enable the Canadian industry to supply the cars which are now being imported from abroad. That was substantially his point. Is the hon. member aware that the excise tax is applied also to imported cars, and in the light of that fact will he kindly explain how the removal of the excise tax is going to have any bearing on the importation of cars from abroad?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is really not particularly relevant to the subject, nor to the figures which I quoted. There is a difference between an imported vehicle being sold for $2,000 and one made in Canada and sold for $3,000. There is an excise

figure of approximately $90. I can substantiate that, and I shall do so if my hon. friend wants an example.
I suggest that the government should give serious consideration to the production of the Bobcat, which is an amphibious vehicle developed by the Department of National Defence and engineers of the Canada Car Company, whose plant in Fort William would be in the immediate position to proceed with its production. The reason I am advocating that this vehicle be used for the opening up of the far north is that until recently it was the objective of the government, and now it seems to be totally ignored.
Those of us who were hoping to see a budget designed to create jobs for the unemployed certainly could not cheer. Only the day before the budget Chrysler Corporation of Canada announced that some 3,500 workers were being laid off in a shut-down of all passenger car production. Some of these will return to work, while others will be laid off indefinitely. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Fort William Times-Journal of April 2, which indicates a serious and alarming unemployment situation. I am going to quote only a paragraph:
An all-time record high of 10,527 people are seeking employment according to figures which reached the lakehead employment advisory committee during their March meeting.
The move to amalgamate the telegraph services at Fort William, which cannot be assessed but as a step toward a program to merge all telegraph services across the country, is just a beginning of a nation-wide scheme to bring about the physical amalgamation of the two railways, a proposal which was originated by the Conservative government of R. B. Bennett in the 1930's. Only last week at a meeting of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, attended by the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, and some of his officials, it was brought out that extensive reductions in service on sections of the line to Sioux Lookout and between Atikokan and Rainy River were effected, as well as at Reddit, Armstrong, Nakina and Longlac, and Belleville in the eastern part of the province of Ontario. As a result Sioux Lookout, a railway town dependent for its existence upon the Canadian National Railways, will be on the verge of becoming a ghost town. I am told that the morale among the men in those sections of the Canadian National railway system has never been as low as it is at the present time.
It is all very well to be pleased with a budget which forecasts a surplus, but with nearly 800,000 unemployed the satisfaction
The Budget-Mr. Badanai is but of short duration. I have had occasion to say, and I say it again, that I would rather see deficit financing, with full employment of the available manpower of the country than a financial statement in the black with massive unemployment. Our human resources are paramount, and their welfare should be the first consideration of any government. I do not mean to imply that those who are occupying the treasury benches are less concerned with the welfare of the people. I suggest that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues have been listening to the wrong prophets and, for whatever reason, have not been able to come up with the right answer to cure unemployment, and that these trends toward amalgamations or mergers of services will not produce results acceptable to the Canadian people.
On February 18 I asked the Minister of Finance whether he would consider the removal of the burden of double taxation on those people who have received or will receive payments under the Ontario health plan and who cannot deduct those medical expenses from their taxable income even though they have paid taxes on their contributions to the plan. The minister informed the house that it was not appropriate to discuss fiscal policy during the question period. Now I expect it to be quite in order for me or for any other member to ask the minister, since the federal government contributes only a portion of the cost of this plan, whether some adjustment could not be made so the provincial and personal share of these payments might be deducted from taxable income.
To illustrate my point, prior to January, 1959 a person who was covered for hospitalization and medical care under Blue Cross paid $5.40 per annum more than he is paying for his present coverage under the Ontario hospital plan and Blue Cross for semiprivate and P.S.I. medical. In 1958 he was allowed to deduct all hospital expenses from his taxable income. In 1959 this person was hospitalized twice, but he can deduct only his semiprivate room charge of $3 per day instead of the full charge of $23.25 per day. This means that instead of having a tax refund of $45.70 for 1959 he is allowed a refund of only $5.70. In other words the government charged the extra $40 against its contribution of only one third of the cost of hospitalization.
I express the sincere hope that in what the minister did not spell out in his statement last Thursday, when he said that minor adjustments will be made, he had this particular feature in mind.

The Budget-Mr. Badanai
On Friday, March 18 I asked the Minister of National Revenue whether the government had made any attempt to evaluate the impact that the selling of duty and tax free goods by International Resort Facilities Limited to United States tourists at border points is going to have on small retail merchants who derive their livelihood from the tourist trade. A few days later the minister replied to the effect that it was impossible to determine the impact of that business because operations had not yet started.
This is a question which has engaged the attention of the tourist industry as well as the retail merchants association. It has been reported that this scheme may well cost Canada a lot of money as a result of the dislocation of small businesses and the diversion of customs duties and sales tax revenue from the federal treasury.
The Minister of National Revenue also indicated in his reply that the company involved, namely International Resort Facilities Limited, was incorporated in the regular way under the Canadian Companies Act. This is, of course, not a question of legality but of whether or not this type of free shops merchandising is in the national interest. These shops will be stocked with samples of imported goods, cameras, perfumes, watches and clothing. While Canadian goods will probably be on display, the visitor will be tempted to buy goods imported from abroad and brought into this country in bond so they can be sold without customs and excise taxes.
Theoretically any merchant could set up a bonded warehouse, but in practice small retailers could not afford such an overhead, with the result that they will be the losers in competition for the tourist dollars. Those feeling the effects of these free shops will be not only merchants operating at border cities anywhere in Canada, but the chief losers will be a large section of our national retailers. I suggest that a close study be made of this new type of merchandising which might cause more trouble than the extra dollars are worth to the country even if, indeed, it should mean extra revenues, something which I doubt.
About a year ago, on the occasion of a debate on a supply motion, the Leader of the Opposition introduced the subject of Canadian-United States relations and during the course of that debate I mentioned the move by the city of Chicago to have an increase in the diversion of water from lake Michigan from 1,500 to 2,500 cubic feet per second, the effect of which would have been a threat to the water levels of the great lakes. You will recall that the bill passed the United States Senate, but fortunately it
[Mr. Badanai.1
was vetoed by the President. Now they are at it again, and I do not know whether this government can stem the tide. I therefore wonder whether a proposal formulated in the mind of one of our brilliant young engineers, namely Mr. Thomas Kierans, who hails from the city of Sudbury, has sufficient merit for this government to give it serious consideration.
Briefly, the plan would be to take fresh water from rivers flowing into James bay and divert it by way of the Harricanaw river into the Ottawa and Mattawa rivers, lake Nipis-sing and the French river into Georgian bay; in stages, up to 25,000 cubic feet of water per second would be diverted. The beginning stage calls for the diversion of about 4,000 cubic feet of water per second from the Bell river to the Harricanaw river near the height of land south of James bay. This initial diversion, according to Mr. Kierans' estimate, could be completed within three to four years.
What Mr. Kierans suggests, however, is a study which would determine the feasibility of the plan. Mr. Kierans submitted his original idea to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Unfortunately the minister's reaction was negative. On the other hand the reaction of Robert Macaulay, minister of energy and resources in the Ontario provincial government, was receptive, so much so that Mr. Macaulay has initiated a study of the plan with his energy committee and with Ontario hydro.
Inasmuch as the United States government is plagued by the continuing problem of water diversion from the great lakes by the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois, the plan was taken to Washington by Mr. Robert Evans of Sudbury. There Mr. Evans was received by Senator Fulbright, chairman of the Senate foreign relations committee; by Senator Paul Douglas of Illinois and Senator Alexander Wiley of Wisconsin. Senator Douglas is working hard to secure more water for his state. Senator Wiley is emphatically opposed to further diversion.
There is pending now before the Senate foreign	relations	committee	a	bill	called
H.	R. 1, which calls for a study of the Chicago
water diversion problem, while at the same time it would permit Chicago to divert 1,000 cubic feet per second more of water from the great lakes.	That city	is	at present
taking 1,500 cubic feet per second for sanitary and shipping purposes, and an additional
I,	800 cubic feet per second for domestic clear water purposes.
The bill already has passed the house and should	be reported out from	the	Senateforeign	relations	committee	to	the	Senate

He told Mr. Evans he would recommend that the United States initiate funds to study its feasibility, with the permission and co-operation of Canada. I understand that the Prime Minister has been informed of the plan. I would therefore suggest to the Minister of Finance that he make money available, if necessary, for initiating a study of this plan with the co-operation of the United States.
Mr. Kierans prepared a substantial brief, a copy of which I believe is in the hands of the Prime Minister. I am just quoting from one page of it. It contains that proposal and suggests that the advantages that project could offer to Canada include the following:
(a)	Profit from the sale of water to certain water deficient areas in North America.
(b)	Hydroelectric energy from the fall of the new water on the southern side of the height of land.
(c)	A barge navigation channel from James bay to the great lakes and the lower Ottawa, thus providing a low cost transportation system for the large iron ore reserves of the James bay area.
(d)	An opportunity to open for economic development a very large area of Canada now only very sparsely settled.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance acknowledged the demand made upon the government for devaluation of the Canadian dollar to the level of the United States dollar. As reported at page 2673 of Hansard he had this to say:
There is a related question upon which I should like to dwell for a moment. This is the question of our exchange rate. The external price of our Canadian dollar has been high for eight years now and is currently running about 5 per cent above the United States dollar. The situation has been brought about mainly as a result of an inflow of foreign capital and reflects the confidence of outsiders in the soundness of the management of our financial affairs. Admittedly it lowers the prices received in Canadian dollars by those exporters who have to sell in world markets at world prices.
Further on the same page he continued:
It might well be that the government could not reduce the inflow of funds sufficiently without imposing direct controls on capital movements and then on the movement of goods. Apart from the economic objections to such policies it would be a very difficult matter to work out effective technical means of control. Even then the controls would not be effective unless the objective were one which commanded the broad public support which is necessary for general compliance. In other words we would be embarking upon a gigantic financial speculation with no assurance of success.
With that statement the minister is attempting to give this question an air of finality which should not be raised now or ever, at least until the government will decide when it will be appropriate for further review. The minister contended' that the inflow of foreign capital was responsible for
The Budget-Mr. Badanai the premium on the Canadian dollar, but said nothing about the borrowing in the United States by provincial governments and municipalities and private corporations, a procedure which many would agree to have been chiefly the result of poor financial management. It is a statement which does not take into consideration the artificial value of the dollar which in reality, having regard to its true value in relation to our trade deficit, should be worth only 95 cents instead of $1.05 in United States dollars. I think the truth of the matter can be found in the suggestion that the Canadian dollar is presently being manipulated by a few international financiers.
The artificial value of our dollar is damaging our tourist industry to the tune of millions of dollars. It has severely handicapped northwestern Ontario major industries, pulp and paper and forest products, and the iron ore from Steep Rock iron mines. I submit to the minister that he would render Canada an excellent service if he would reconsider the question in the light of what parity of our dollar with that of the United States would mean to our export trade and to the development of Canada.
In the matter of civil service salaries, the minister made an astonishing statement to the effect that the last general increase in civil service salaries was authorized by the present government in July, 1957. He very conveniently omitted to say that the general increase had been proposed and approved by the government of the previous prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, as of May of that year, several days before the then prime minister decided to resign. The increase at that time ranged from 3J to 12 per cent, or an average of 6 per cent. On the same date increases to the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were also granted. After the brush-off which the civil service received from the present government last year we at least anticipated that in this year's budget a general increase would be forthcoming for all civil service employees, not only for a fraction of the number who will benefit by the minister's announcement. Perhaps among those hardest hit by this omission are the postal employees who are actually in receipt of a lower net income than they enjoyed three years ago.
There is another important omission about which the minister failed even to whisper; that is, giving civil servants who do not occupy executive positions the right to bargain, in the same way as members of police forces and firemen, and the protection that none should suffer the penalty of dismissal

The Budget-Mr. Badanai for attending a political meeting. The granting of these rights would remove the stigma of being considered second class citizens subject to penalties and loss of employment. As far as the civil service is concerned, this budget can be labelled the half a loaf budget of 1960 to be divided among a fraction of the civil service body.
On January 20, on orders of the day, I asked the Minister of Finance if he would inform the house whether a borrower from the industrial development bank could prepay a loan without having to pay a penalty, and if not why not. The minister's answer was to the effect that the industrial development bank is a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada and that he, as Minister of Finance, had no control over it.
The reason which prompted me to ask the question was that a firm in my constituency, on whose lands and buildings the industrial development bank loaned $60,000 on a mortgage, recently had sold a part of their assets consisting of small boats which they manufactured, some machinery and stock. Consequently they wished to prepay the sum of $25,000 on the mortgage; and all things considered, when money is still in a strait-jacket this prepayment or any prepayment of loans should be welcomed by the government-owned bank. But because the mortgage contained a clause under which the bank reserved the right to charge a premium on prepayments which amounted to one tenth of one per cent, multiplied by the number of months in advancement of the date the instalments fell due, the premium asked was excessive. The manager of the company wrote a letter asking me to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance in the hope that he would see the merit of the request, which resulted in the question and answer as reported in Hansard of January 20 last, pages 135 and 136.
I did, however, receive a detailed explanation from the secretary of the industrial development bank, which contained the following paragraph:
Many mortgage lenders do not permit prepayment of mortgages at all and where prepayment is permitted, it is the usual practice to charge a prepayment fee whenever any amount is prepaid.
This would mean, then, that the government-owned industrial development bank has adopted the practice and regulations of ordinary moneylenders. It is a matter of regret that the minister overlooked the importance of suggesting an amendment of this practice to the industrial development bank. The statement of profit and loss for the year ending September, 1959 reported a rather healthy profit of $1,533,363, and an amendment which would remove the objectionable

feature of premiums on prepayments of loans would in no way prejudice the profit position and purpose of the bank.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this budget, and I am very pleased and proud to do so. We have a courageous budget introduced by a courageous and capable minister. This budget, as has been well said, stands to hold the line. At a time like this holding the line is a necessary thing. We have to learn to live within our means. We have been living beyond our means, but now we are going to stand and move forward from here. I compliment our minister and the government for taking this stand, which every thinking man in Canada knows has to be taken.
I am pleased, however, to see that even in this year of holding the line we have not forgotten the great body of civil servants who run our country so efficiently. As usual the members of "the group" have criticised the stated contribution to this effort. They say "too late and too little". The sum of $15 million, I might point out, is only the minimum set aside for this purpose and, as has been promised by the government, a full review of the civil service is being made and many groups will benefit in the near future.
Amongst these no doubt will be the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This body of men have been notoriously underpaid ever since 1873. I would say that the basic pay is now more realistic, but there are still certain groups within that body, notably the sergeants and the superintendents, who are underpaid. Bearing in mind the responsibilities they hold and the service they are giving to this country I would recommend to the government that when they are making this review they give special consideration to these particular groups. I served for some 23 years with the mounted police; therefore I speak with firsthand information.
Although I have no doubt that we are moving forward and will continue to move forward, there is still one part of the population which has not come fully into its own, and that is the agriculture industry. In particular I refer to the small family farm. The bureau of statistics assures us that the family farm is now getting a fair share of the national income. I do not think this is quite accurate. I think agriculture has gone forward, and that total income has increased. However, we have an inequity in the agricultural picture. I see a tendency to return to the feudal system in agriculture, not on account of claims of birth or blood but on account of the claims of finance. Today our farms are highly mechanized. Today a farmer

needs a lot of capital, and it is not easy in a free economy to make capital available down to the level of the family farm.
I have consulted with farm groups who have come from all across Canada, and have tried to get them to define the family farm. They refuse to do so, and I think this failure is due to the fact that the better-off farmers are able to use their influence within their own groups to press for those things in agriculture which help the men with the most money. This tends to concentrate agricultural income into fewer and fewer hands, regardless of the increased income available to agriculture generally.
At this point I would ask permission to have the following tables printed in Hansard. The source is the dominion bureau of statistics
The Budget-Mr. Bigg census of Canada, and the tables purport to give the over-all figures of the number of farms in Canada in 1941, 1951 and 1956, and the number of farm holdings by size of farms in 1951 and 1956. These tables are too long to read at this time, and I think it would be for the convenience of the house if they were inserted in the record.

maintopic: TABLE 2. FARM HOLDINGS BY SIZE OF FARM, FOR CANADA, 1951 AND 1956
speechtext:
These tables show that there has been a great decline in the number of farms in Canada. Total acreage has not declined, but the number of farms has notably decreased with one exception, namely that in British Columbia the number of small holdings has increased.
This tendency to increase the size of our farms has a great many backers. The economists agree almost unanimously that the larger farms are more efficient. This means, of course, that you can produce more hogs in a large pen, more chickens in a large chicken house, and more cattle on a large ranch, with a corresponding reduction in the cost per head. It is also true that you can reduce the cost of grain per bushel as acreage increases.
I spent a good many years on a farm. I love the land, and so do most Canadians. It is not sentiment alone that gives us an attachment to the soil; it is a natural way of life. The small farmer on his own land is the happiest man in the world. He is healthy. He works hard. He produces natural wealth. He sleeps well, and he raises his family in the finest of surroundings. I can speak for the people in my district, some 65,000 strong, and say that our whole economy is based on the family farm.
I wish to bring to the attention of every person in Canada the fact that today the number of farmers is shrinking; the number of farm homes is declining; the number of children reared in rural surroundings is becoming fewer and fewer. Dollar efficiency is not the only question involved. We still want to draw on the farms for young men and young women who are healthy, strong and independent. I think this is an environment which must be retained. A few dollars today, properly invested in agriculture at the proper level, would help to do this.
This government is not approaching this question blindly. We have thought long and hard about this subject. A large number of hon. members who sit in this house today have a rural background, and we are trying hard to find a correct compromise between so-called efficiency and this rural way of life. I would have expected greater support from hon. members who have socialist views. They must see this trend, and at times they should be able to see that money wisely spent will help to accomplish what they claim they hope to accomplish, an even distribution of wealth. The program of this government is based on the retention of the family farm. Canada is still an agricultural country, and it is an agricultural exporting country.
Here again we have a double problem. If we decide to support the family farm this


will mean it is likely to cost more to produce our goods, which will then be more difficult to sell in a fiercely competitive world market. However, I think we can achieve a happy medium. If we retain the family farm and still make sure that we produce beyond our needs and turn these products loose on the markets of the world, we can stabilize our economy at home and still be a blessing to the world at large. In order to accomplish this we have to make sure that the family farm is secure, and that is why we have gone in for support prices. We would have no need for support prices were our markets capable of absorbing the whole of our production. But it is hard to get the money down to the family farms when it is being picked up by the corporations who are competing.
We instituted a system of price support for hogs. What happened? Money poured out of the cities, and the farmers were offered an illusory security. They were told that if they worked hard for the corporations they would make more money and be more secure than they would be on their own. Then when the hog market collapsed in the circumstances-because this system always results in overproduction-the corporations withdrew their money from the market. The farmer was unemployed. He rushed to the city, and we find him on the unemployment rolls. If he had stayed on his farm and we had been able to assist him to remain independent, this would not have occurred. It seems to me that our Department of Agriculture has done well to realize that the only way to stop this process is to set a quota on hogs and reduce government support to 100 units. This is not foolproof but it does tend to cut down the extent of vertical integration in the hog industry.
There are one or two other matters I should like to deal with concerning what may be done beyond the home front. Trade is our life blood, and anything we can do to balance our trade will attack this problem from another direction. If we can retain and increase our world markets there will be a greater call for all our agricultural products, and then perhaps there will be a future even for corporation farming. In order to do this we must take steps to reduce the cost of marketing our grain, of transporting it to the lakehead and across the ocean. This must be done more cheaply and efficiently. Anything we can do to diversify our agriculture should be done. We should encourage the growth of things like rapeseed for use in the production of edible and lubricating oil. If we can get our rapeseed put on Crowsnest pass freight

rates it will not only increase the return to the farmer but will make rapeseed oil competitive in the world markets.
Rapeseed is important at the present time in terms of our trade with Japan. Japan has been taking all the rapeseed we can produce. The production of rapeseed in western Canada is leaping ahead. If we can encourage farmers to put rapeseed into production in place of wheat in relation to certain acreages it will help us balance our trade, because rapeseed sells in the world market.
Transportation is very important in getting our goods to market. In my district of Athabasca I cannot exaggerate the necessity of improved transportation facilities. In an area of 60,000 square miles, three quarters of my district is absolutely without road communication of any kind. We do not even have air communication in a great many districts. At Fort Chipewyan, a community of 1,200 people, there is no road, no railway and no airstrip. It is true that in the summer one can land on the lake and in the winter when the lake freezes over it is possible to land on the icy surface, but for a period ranging from eight to ten weeks during the year this community of 1,200 people is completely cut off. We are going ahead with organizing the district so the community can take on the responsibility of a municipal airport.
The description I have given clearly indicates that Canada is still a pioneer country. These people are not whining for government help, but they do have to have it. The government must assist them in building the necessary facilities, just as we built the railroads for their fathers and grandfathers.
Roads still remain the most important link. As all hon. members know, roads are principally the responsibility of a province, but the government of the great province of Alberta has consistently refused to assist in the outlying districts, particularly in the northeast corner of the province.
If roads are to be built the federal government will have to assist in their construction. I think it has a perfectly good reason for doing so, because in the northeastern part of Alberta we have some of the finest tourist country in the whole of Canada. We have Wood Buffalo park with 15,000 buffalo. We have some of the finest fishing lakes in the world and some of the best hunting in the country. This is virgin territory with no roads, railways or other transportation. If the federal government were to assist in putting roads in there tourists, and particularly tourists from the United States, would flock in.
The Budget-Mr. Bigg
Some hon. members might wonder why I mention this in relation to trade, but tourist dollars are solid dollars. This is the most important kind of trade we can get at present to balance our trade with the United States. We want tourists, and in large numbers. We are not selling tourism in Canada as we should. We do not advertise the attractions of our country, and we do not even stay home and enjoy our own country. We spend far too much abroad which could be spent at home. All hon. members from eastern constituencies have a standing invitation to visit us in Alberta in September. We want you to come, and when you return we want you to tell everyone what you saw. When hon. members have done so people will come out west in large numbers.
It is useless to talk about agriculture, trade and the need for improved transportation if we do not have peace, and so I come down to the last and I think possibly the most important subject facing us today, the peace of the world and the defence of our nation. I suggest that this subject can be handled under two headings. We must be strong at home and we must be generous abroad. I am greatly assured, after hearing the speech of the Minister of National Defence, that we have a realistic approach to the defence of North America. If we keep North America strong and free it will serve as a launching pad for the peace of the world. Nothing less than a realistic approach to the defence of this continent is of any value. This is the time not for pacifism but for realism. It is a time to get ourselves in shape, physically, mentally and spiritually to accept this challenge. I repeat, we must be strong at home and generous abroad.
To be strong at home we need a strong air force. To understand what I mean you have only to visit Cold Lake airport, one of the finest airports in the world. You should see the morale of the men there in the Royal Canadian Air Force, the finest air force in the world. These boys are worried about the future of aviation and of the air force. I have told them and the Minister of National Defence has also told them that we are going to keep them flying. We are going to supply them with the finest up to date aircraft we can, bearing in mind our ability to produce and pay for such planes. I believe we will always need them. These boys are willing to fly the planes and, as I have said, I have assured them we will do everything in our power to see that they keep their wings. So much for the need of our being strong at home.
As my second point I mentioned that we must be generous abroad. We in Canada

The Budget-Mr. Carter have learned complete tolerance. We are going to love our neighbour in a completely practical way. We intend to do our best to feed him. We have a future here in Canada to produce all the food we can as cheaply as we can and give it to the people of the world as quickly and as inexpensively as we can; but in order to do this we must bear in mind that charity begins at home. We want to take a long look at the family farm and make sure our agricultural policies are long term policies that will keep the farm family on the farm.
I think the most forward step we have taken in that direction to date has been through the provision of acreage payments. We have given the small family farmer a little shot in the arm, a bit of assistance, but it is not enough. The farmers are in need, and perhaps particularly those in my district where they have sustained three crop failures in a row and are hard pressed. I would strongly urge upon the government that again in this year of holding the line wo do not hold it too rigidly. I urge the government to see that the family farmer receives temporary support when he needs it. In my opinion he still requires this assistance to help him get back on his feet and keep him in the running.
If we take action in this regard then our policies of price supports, farm credit, emergency assistance for crops under the snow, crop insurance, land protection and rehabilitation, irrigration and all the measures we have undertaken will work out to the advantage of all Canadians. If we have a strong and healthy farm community at home we will be in a position to assist those in underdeveloped countries who require our aid.

Mr. Speaker, the budget speech affords the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) an opportunity to review the national accounts of the year which has passed, to describe the financial health of the nation, and in general to give an accounting of the government's stewardship in handling the nation's business. In an economy such as ours which is based mainly on free enterprise the main duty of the government is to create as far as possible a favourable economic climate wherein free men by exercising their free decisions can operate the various kinds of business with a minimum of interference and a maximum of success.
The budget speech should therefore provide clear and accurate information in a simple form so as to be readily accessible to the public. It should also contain an accurate account of all the financial activities of the government, a forecast of the economic


weather that is likely to be encountered during the coming year, and it should indicate what adjustments the government is making to meet the situation and what part the public will have to play in this regard as well.
Since no government plans or action can be successful without the wholehearted cooperation of the people it is important that the people not only know and understand what defects exist in our economy but also how they came about, what forces caused them and how these forces can be neutralized or reversed.
If we appraise the budget by these standards I think it is fair to say that while it does contain a few items that will be welcomed by the Canadian people it also has some glaring deficiencies which will cause a great deal of disappointment to thinking people who are looking for clear, positive leadership at this very crucial period in our history. I would not wish for one minute to detract any credit or commendation from the minister for his efforts to achieve a balanced budget or for his easing of the double impact of the estate and income tax on the widows and children of deceased taxpayers.
I welcome also the increased payments to the lower paid civil servants. True, it is only an item of $15 million and only about 50,000 or one third of the total civil service force will benefit from it. Still it is better than nothing and I commend the minister for doing even that. But I must tell him at the same time that it destroys the argument that he used on a former occasion when he turned down a request of the civil service because of the high cost to the government as he stated at that time. Fifteen million dollars is not a very huge expenditure and if we can afford it this year I think we could very well have afforded it last year and perhaps have alleviated a great deal of the hardship which some of these poorly paid civil servants have had to undergo in the meantime.
The minister's efforts to enable us to live better electrically will no doubt be welcomed by people setting up new homes. It will help in some measure to reduce the cost of furnishing homes and in that way offset the rising costs due to the high interest rates that have to be paid on mortgages. But while giving the minister full marks for all these points, we cannot assess them at their true value unless we know their true cost and also know the motive that lies behind them.
It is interesting to note that a surplus, which was denounced as something very wicked by the minister and his party prior to the 1957 election, has now seemed to

acquire at least a small measure of virtue. I do not know whether the virtue is to be measured by the size of the surplus. If so, we hope it will grow. But the difference between a $12 million deficit and a $12 million surplus will have a rather negligible effect on the economy and if that surplus is being acquired at the expense of hardship to certain individual Canadians or at the expense of the development of certain underdeveloped parts of our country, then I think we may very likely be paying too high a price for it. Also, if it is being acquired at the expense of an increase in veterans war pensions, which is more urgently needed at this time than in any past year, then again I doubt whether it is worth the cost. If in addition to this cost the motive behind it is purely political so that a balanced budget can be achieved before the next election, then, of course, that destroys its worth completely.
As the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) pointed out yesterday, there is a great deal of disappointment that the budget indicates that nothing is to be done to ease the cost of production in the fishing industry. The suggestions made by the fisheries council of Canada in this regard have not received favourable consideration. They were very modest requests and not only very practical but vital to the welfare of the fishing industry. The removal of the tax on diesel fuel would not mean a very large cost to the federal treasury but it would wipe out a great deal of discrimination between different types of fishing vessels and at the same time would enable the fish to be produced more cheaply. Not even the insignificant request that the tax be removed on diesel oil used in generating electricity within the fishing industry has received favourable consideration even though this privilege is and has been enjoyed by the mining industry for some years. The cost of drying fish is one of the main factors which will decide whether or not we can compete in foreign markets. The removal of the sales tax on imported driers and imported parts for maintenance would again be a great help to the fishing industry, but no special consideration has been given to any of these requests.
Also, there is nothing in the budget to indicate any encouragement of the development of our resources in the Atlantic provinces. There are no special tax incentives to induce enterprises to establish themselves in the maritimes and no word as to whether there is to be a modification of the industrial development bank or whether a development corporation is to be set up to introduce a measure of flexibility into our economy.
The Budget-Mr. Carter Therefore we must conclude from the budget that the maritimes, or the Atlantic provinces, must still bear the full brunt of the bad effect of tight money and, at the same time, there will be no easing of the dollar premium which is a great handicap to our fish exporters who sell to the United States markets.
It seems to me that the main criticism of the budget is that it does not show any positive leadership. There is no recognition of the problems, no reappraisal, agonizing or otherwise, of the government's policies and no redirection of our economy.
The problems of the uneven development of our resources, to which I have just referred, which is a direct result of tight money and high interest rates; the growing hard core of the unemployed during relative prosperity; the pattern of unemployment which involves a much higher percentage of the work force in the Atlantic provinces than in other parts of Canada; the dangerous balance of our trade payments, especially in so far as invisible exports are concerned; our mounting debt, public and private; the high interest rates which have been frozen for some years to come by the uncallable bonds that the minister has put on the market; the effects that we must expect through automation; all of these problems have been entirely ignored. Apparently the government is operating on the principle that if we ignore them and leave them alone long enough they will go away of their own accord.
On this score the government has no reason to be proud of its stewardship. We know from the budget that the government's estimated expenditures for the coming year amount to $5,880 million. If we look at the estimates for 1957-58, which were the last estimates introduced by the former administration, we find that the estimated expenditures were $4,827 million, exactly $1 billion less. If we study the budget papers, at page 19 we find that the total federal expenditure for 1959 amounted to $6,359 million, and that the figure for 1957 was $5,337 million, again an increase of $1 billion in expenditures since this government took office.
If we look at page 18 of the budget papers and study the effect on the taxpayer and if we exclude the investment income we find that the total amount of money taken from the taxpayers in 1957 was roughly $5,300 million, but last year the government took $334 million more than this. If the minister's estimates are right for the coming year and are as accurate as he has boasted about last year's estimates, then he will take an extra $592 million from the Canadian taxpayers. I emphasize these figures, Mr. Speaker, because they come ill from a government which made
2922	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Carter so much fuss about waste and extravagance prior to the 1957 election, and which was elected on a firm pledge to cut expenditures by $500 million; a government which had also pledged not only to cut expenditures but to cut taxes as well. Therefore, these figures are interesting in that they highlight the wide discrepancy between the promises of this government before election and their performance since election.
If we look at the public debt-again on the same page of the budget papers-we find the same picture. In 1957 the interest on the public debt was $519 million; in 1959 it was $678 million, or $150 million more. If we look at the estimates for 1960-61 we find that the interest on the public debt is estimated at $774 million, which means an extra $250 million, which is going to be, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) pointed out yesterday, a millstone which will hang around the necks of Canadians for many years to come.
It is unfortunate that we have so little information concerning private debt. I placed a question on the order paper some time ago and the answer, as recorded at page 2383 of Hansard, showed that in 1949 the total consumer debt of Canadians amounted to $582 million, but in 1959 the consumer debt of Canadians had increased to $2,076 million. These figures are not exactly comparable because they are different kinds of dollars. But if we reduce the $2,076 million of 1959 into 1949 dollars we get $1,490 million, which means an increase of $900 million in consumer debt during the last 10 years. Not only has consumer debt and public debt both increased, but interest rates have increased as well.
At page 2672 of Hansard the minister made reference to productivity. He said the following:
We must place emphasis on greater productivity and efficiency rather than on sheer size, on cost control rather than on price increases, on greater saving rather than on excessive consumption.
I have been interested in this question of productivity for some time. I spent a whole week end in the library trying to discover information on this subject. Unfortunately, however, there does not seem to be any information available. We do not know what our man-hour productivity is here in Canada either in general terms or in specific industries. We do not even know what manhours are worked each year. However, we know that the gross national product has increased by 3J per cent. If we take into consideration the number of people who have had jobs during the year, it would appear that there is a slight increase in our productivity. But when we take into account


the extra productivity in the agriculture industry, it is doubtful whether there has been any actual increase in productivity in the other sectors of our economy.
This question of productivity is of immense importance because unless we have some information about it we shall not be able to measure the effects of automation on productivity when its impact is fully felt. At present automation has not had a great effect on Canadian industry. For most Canadian small businesses automation machines are too expensive to be employed by them. However, the time is coming when these machines will be much cheaper and will be available to small industries. That day may not be far distant. A radio report this morning indicated that it might come within the next 10 years. When it comes it is going to bring with it a whole new set of social and economic problems. What are we doing to prepare for it? Certainly one of the first steps toward the preparation must be to make a study so that we shall have at our disposal accurate information on man-hour productivity in Canadian industry.
The inadequacy of our present economic system is increased by this lack of information. It is further complicated because we do not have an absolute unit with which to measure our wealth. How would we manage if we were obliged to use a yard or a pound that was different every year? No scientific progress was possible until absolute physical standards were evolved for length, weight and volume. Yet we measure our wealth in terms of a dollar that changes, not only from year to year but during the year as well. In fact, it changes practically every day in the year.
We are living in times when it is imperative that business firms and industry should be able to make rapid and accurate comparisons of cost control, price increases, efficiency and productivity at very short notice. But how can this be done with a unit that is constantly changing? Then again the dollar is not only a unit for measuring wealth, it is in addition a medium of exchange and on some occasions a commodity bought and sold on the world market. This situation raises a question as to whether these functions are compatible with each other. Should we not therefore have a royal commission to look into this subject and bring forward recommendations that can be used at least to introduce a measure of simplicity into our system?
In conclusion I should like to commend the minister for the little bit of indirect advice-

he gave to the people of Canada as reported at page 2672 of Hansard. This is what he said:
Canadians can increase their own domestic capital and make this country financially more self-reliant if they are prepared to practise increased efficiency, productivity and thrift.
Then he goes on to say this, and this is the punch line:
This responsibility falls on all levels of government, private business and individuals.
And, I presume, on the minister himself. It is true that we can do this as Canadians and we should do it. However, I think the burning question is this: Will we do it? When we are obliged to choose between the national interest and our own narrow selfinterest do we as Canadians have sufficient self-discipline to put the national interest first?
I raised this question in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping a week or so ago. Mr. Donald Gordon complimented me on my altruism but he went on to say that in the hard bargaining that goes on between labour and management in working out their agreements he felt it is a little overoptimistic to expect that the national interest should be the overriding factor. However, unless the national interest becomes the overriding factor, these suggestions which the minister made will not produce any tangible effect.
Some time ago the Duke of Edinburgh called attention to our lack of physical fitness and most people in Canada agreed with him. Many editorials were written in praise and support of what the duke said. However, I think we need to ask ourselves whether this physical softness-if this physical softness is a fact-is not a reflection of our inner softness, our moral softness, our mental softness, our reluctance to do any hard thinking. If this is a fact, is it not true that most of our economic problems can be traced directly to this source?
We Canadians need to ask ourselves whether we are not a self-indulgent, pleasureseeking, security-minded people, whether we are able to distinguish between our wants and our needs and whether we have the necessary self-discipline to make the right decision with the right motive.
As I was coming to work this morning I met a friend who told me a story about a farmer, and he used this story to illustrate the people's attitude toward government. This story came to my mind as I listened to the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) who preceded me in this debate. Illustrating the people's attitude toward government generally, he pointed to a litter of pigs in his pen and said, "That is just like it: those that
The Budget-Mr. MacRae are not sucking are squealing". And there may be a lot of truth in that statement.
In any case, if the minister's suggestions are going to bear any fruit, what Canada must have is a new concept of living, a new sense of purpose, and above all a new unifying idea which will enable us all to rise and work concertedly together, not only in the national interest but in the interests of the world as a whole.
Two weeks ago there was distributed to every home in Canada a little pamphlet called "Ideology and Co-Existence". I hope every Canadian will read this pamphlet not once but many times, because it not only describes the problems of mental softness and moral softness and the dangers inherent in them, but it also provides the answers to those problems as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words in contribution to this debate must be to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) upon his budget and his presentation of it. There is no question that in the next few weeks, perhaps the next few months, there will be many things said about this budget, many things complimentary and many things which are not complimentary. But over the week end I read these words in one of Canada's greatest newspapers in describing the budget which had been brought down. This newspaper said, "It was sound, it was solid, it was business-like and it was competent". I think those words are most applicable not only to the budget, to the minister and to his handling of his department, but also to the government of this country as it is constituted today.
In discussing the points which are brought out in the budget there are only two that I would like to discuss at this time. The first is the raise given to the civil servants. I think a very fine thing was done by this government in giving a raise to 50,000 clerks and those who are lower paid. I think they will welcome it; I am sure they will. I know that the representations which I have had from my own constituency in which there is a fairly high percentage of civil servants have been most reasonable at all times, and I know they will welcome this particular move on the part of the government. I think, too, that the review of civil service salaries in cycles and by groups is the correct and proper way to approach this particular problem.
I am distressed, as I am sure most thinking Canadians are, by the attitude which has been taken by certain of the leaders of the civil service association and the civil service federation. The language they have used as

The Budget-Mr. MacRae reported in the press over the last months is something you would expect to see perhaps in the Canadian Sailor, or something of that category. Of course, I am sure these gentlemen are honourable people, but they are trying to justify their own salaries as all union leaders try to justify their salaries. I think they have said many things which should never have been said. They should realize that this government will not be bludgeoned and bullied into doing anything. I think all Canadians are learning that the government will treat everyone fairly at all times.
There was another point brought out in the budget, and that was the relief given to the textile industry, especially to cotton milling firms. That was especially interesting to me because in my constituency we have a small cotton milling town which has been having a rather difficult time. We used to say years ago that you should never reinforce failure. Well, you should not, but I do not think the textile industry in this country should yet be considered a failure. I think it can be saved even in the face of competition from Japan, United States and other countries. This measure was most welcome to me and I am sure to the people of my constituency also.
For the few minutes I have today I should like to discuss a subject which is very dear to my heart, and that is the economy of Atlantic Canada, our maritime economy. I suppose that Upper Canadians, or sometimes we just call them Canadians, are tired of listening to this but it is something about which we feel very strongly. All of those who live in Atlantic Canada are interested in that part of the country and wish to stay there. Their roots are there and they would like to have their families remain there. We know that at confederation the maritime provinces were the most wealthy part of this country and the most heavily settled. We know, too, that in 1864 they were planning a maritime union. The father of our country, Sir John A. Macdonald, heard of this and hurried down to persuade them that rather than unite they should come into Canada as they were. Then in 1867 New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, along with Upper and Lower Canada, that is, Ontario and Quebec, united to form this great dominion. But this was not accepted by our people entirely. Of course, now they have forgotten, although peoples' memories are long and these things are handed down, but they hung black crepe on the doors in Halifax and Saint John on the first day of July, 1867.
From 1867 up until perhaps 1950 our economy has never been able to keep pace with the rest of Canada. We have dropped


steadily back from an economic point of view. We know, of course, what our contribution has been to this country in war time. Those who met the men who served who came from the maritimes in the two great wars, great numbers of them, know the contribution they made. We all know what their contribution has been in peace. Great political figures have come from the maritimes to lead this country. Nova Scotia provided three prime ministers of Canada including the great Sir Robert Laird Borden. New Brunswick provided Richard Bedford Bennett and a prime minister of Great Britain, Bonar Law. We have provided industrialists, leaders of the church, of professions and education, such as the late Hon. Sidney Smith, so recently deceased, and other men of that calibre.
But this is changing. During the last decade in the maritime provinces there has been progress, and there has been progress for two reasons. I think the first one is that the people of Atlantic Canada are trying to raise themselves economically by their bootstraps. In fact they sometimes refer to it down there as "Operation Bootstrap".
One of the steps taken, and there are two I would like to discuss, has been the meetings of the Atlantic premiers which were instituted some seven or eight years ago, when the premiers of the four Atlantic provinces, regardless of their party affiliation began meeting to try to work out and do something about their mutual problems. Our own able and distinguished premier of New Brunswick, Hon. Hugh John Flemming, has always taken an active and leading part in these conferences.
Then there is another body which I have mentioned before but would like to mention again, the Atlantic provinces economic council, which was founded in 1954. Many things have been said about it, but here is a quotation from one of the Ottawa papers:
The letters "APEC"-
They stand of course for Atlantic provinces economic council.
-spell out a symbol of a new and united determination of the Atlantic provinces to force consideration ... and correction ... of economic problems of that area upon the rest of Canada. This is a citizen body now busily working to inform and consolidate public opinion behind the proposals of the four provincial governments for the development of these provinces.
From their statement of policy I should like to put a few words on record in this house as follows:
What APEC is.
The Atlantic provinces economic council is a voluntary association of industry, business organization and of individuals. Its objective is the raising of the economic status of the Atlantic provinces region.

APEC is non-political and non-profit making. Its basic idea lies in the man with an idea, an organization with a plan, a government with a policy, and is designed to produce economic betterment within the region and the Canadian nation as a whole. Just as in any organization where there are only men, it is always strengthened and made better because women take some part. The women of the Atlantic provinces now have their own women's Atlantic council.
Last September the annual meeting of the Atlantic provinces economic council was held in my home city of Fredericton and I had the opportunity to attend. I was amazed at the amount of work which these businessmen, leaders of the professions and others were doing. It is hoped that at the annual meeting in Halifax this fall there will be in attendance all the maritime senators and members of parliament.
Another excellent step which was taken because of APEC was the formation in London, England of the Atlantic provinces office under a very able businessman, Watson Jamer, who has already been successful in bringing some industry to Atlantic Canada. I was interested in a report in the press with regard to the possibility of further development of mineral sites in northern New Brunswick. Some of us believe there is a reserve of minerals in this area second to none in the world. The mines there which have been quiescent for the last year or two because of economic conditions affecting minerals will be going back into production, and that is most encouraging news to us.
Yes, we are showing initiative now in Atlantic Canada, and we are taking action with regard to our economic problems. We have one of the greatest basic assets-a stable, eager work force. We have electric power, and all we need is industry.
I should like to say that this government has done much for us since 1957. The equalization grants have been of great help in providing the money to do things which otherwise we could not have done; the aid given to our province in respect of electrical development-the building of thermal plants and transmission lines-has also been extremely valuable. I should like to quote a few figures which I have assembled in preparation for my contribution to this debate showing the expenditures in New Brunswick in two contrasting years. I will use the two years 1955, under the previous administration, and 1959. The comparison is interesting.

I have used round figures because I just wanted to point out the things which this government is doing for the Atlantic provinces.
I have, too, a clipping from a recent newspaper containing an article from the Canadian Press which reads as follows:
Private and public investment in the Atlantic provinces is expected to reach a record $563 million in 1960, the Atlantic provinces economic council said today.
I should like to say a word about York-Sunbury, my own constituency. This has been the most successful year, I believe, in the history of that part of New Brunswick. I mentioned earlier how happy the people of Marysville would be over the tariff protection which is now to be accorded to their products. The Minto coal field in central New Brunswick has produced more coal this past year than ever before in its history. The new town of Oromocto beside Camp Gagetown continues to grow. We hope the new Department of Agriculture research station, costing nearly $2 million, will be ready this fall. We are experiencing a building boom second to none in our history.
Unemployment has been mentioned in this house on many occasions. It is true there are men and women who are unemployed in Fredericton as elsewhere, but I should like to tell the house about something that happened a few weeks ago. The daily Gleaner,

The Budget-Mr. MacRae the Fredericton newspaper, offered as a public service to those who were unemployed, the opportunity to advertise in its classified columns without cost it they wanted work. There were some 2,400 men and women drawing unemployment insurance benefits. After a few days had passed, and it had become known in the area that men and women could advertise without cost to themselves in the local paper, I decided to see how many people were actually advertising. The results were interesting. The first day I checked there were 17. The next day there were nine, and of these nine, most were repeats from the day before. One was the advertisement of a lady attempting to get pupils for piano lessons, and another was that of a high school girl who wanted to do baby sitting. I think there is a lesson here which we should take into account when we think of our unemployment figures today.
Another point which I think should be mentioned is this. I do not think unemployment should be used as a political football. I can remember the time after the election of 1957 when perhaps on occasion discussion in this house became acrimonious. In particular, I remember well one night when the opposition asked for unemployment figures. They were given, and they were considerably higher than they had been. As a matter of fact, they were higher than many of us would have liked to see. I recall that there were members of the Liberal opposition at that time who, like Horatius on the bridge, could scarce forbear to cheer. I remember only too well two of them in particular who did cheer at that point, the former hon. member for Portneuf and the former hon. member for Charlotte. Neither of them were here after March 31, 1958.
As I have said, we are raising ourselves by our bootstraps in the maritimes. However, there are one or two matters which I should like to bring to the attention of the government, things which I feel might be done to help us down there. I may say that none of us want any part of Canada to be a second class area. There must be no second class Canadians and no second class areas of Canada. First, I should like to suggest to the government that more defence orders and public service contracts should be allocated to maritime firms. I suggest this might be done along the same lines as it is done in the United States. In each defence department procurement agency there is a small industries division which can set aside all or part of a government order for military supplies for tendering only by small firms if it is felt these companies can do the job. Most of these small industries are to be found in the retarded areas of the country.

In addition, the 6 per cent preference given under the buy American act to United States firms over foreign companies in bidding for government orders is extended to 12 per cent in the case of labour surplus areas. Before awarding any contract for government supplies to a firm in an areas that has no unemployment problems, any bidder from a labour surplus area whose tender has been within 20 per cent of the successful firm is given a second opportunity to match the latter's price and get the order. The federal government's recently instituted policy of calling for tenders from maritime shipyards only for the building of certain vessels for service on the east coast is a step in the right direction.
Second, we hear much about freight rates. It is our firm belief in Atlantic Canada that there must be a revision of the freight rate structure. As there is a royal commission studying this particular matter perhaps it would not be apt at this point to discuss it further but we certainly hope that the commission will see fit to recommend that provision be made for doing something about our freight rates and the difficulties they impose.
With respect to a capital projects program, we have three pet projects in the maritimes at this moment. First there is the Chignecto canal which we sincerely hope engineering and economic studies will prove should be built. I think all hon. members from the Atlantic provinces regardless of party affiliations stand firmly behind it. There may be one or two exceptions but I know that all those who come from New Brunswick stand behind it completely.
The second project is the causeway which, if it were built, would join Canada to Prince Edward Island. There is a difference there, you will see, between joining Prince Edward Island to Canada and joining Canada to Prince Edward Island.
Finally, there is the corridor road project. This is a plan to build a road across central or northern Maine which would link the maritimes with Montreal and central Canada.
I wish to advance the suggestion that provision should be made for low rate capital loans for new industries and the provision of income tax concessions to industries that might locate in the maritime provinces. We have an economic problem there and there is no question about it. I suppose the government of a country can grow too large but I should like to suggest to the distinguished leader of our government that perhaps the time has arrived when there should be appointed a minister of Atlantic affairs just as we have a minister of northern

affairs. We have the problems and we have the men there to solve them under proper direction. If that suggestion were not practical I would suggest as an alternative that a department of government be set up to deal with Atlantic affairs possibly under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). I think that suggestion commends itself and I would ask the government and the distinguished leader of our country to take my suggestions into consideration.
In conclusion, may I say that the decade that has recently concluded has been one of awakening and of renewed hope in Atlantic Canada. Under the able leadership of our Conservative government we are now confident that many of our hopes and aspirations will be achieved in the decade we are now entering.
