Mr. Chairman, the last three or four bills we have considered have involved the same individuals as investigator and as counsel for the petitioner and certain patterns have developed as a result of the functions of these two gentlemen. This case is again one of those in which children are involved. There are two teen age children. There is reference in the evidence to where they have been living, with whom they have been living and so on. I do not wish to suggest that there is anything whatsoever wrong with the existing arrangement. In 1955 the petitioner received a legal separation from the superior court of Quebec and was also awarded custody of the two children at the same time. This couple have been separated since 1949.
From reading the evidence it would appear on the surface at least that the attitude and activities of the respondent or mother were not in the least in keeping with what one would expect of a wife and mother. Apparently she absented herself from the home at times and went with people other than her husband. This behaviour continued for quite some time. She would go away for a few days at a time. They have been separated for some 11 years and the father has had the custody of the children. I do not wish to draw any conclusions with regard to this arrangement but certainly after a separation or divorce, regardless of which parent has legal custody of the children, I think the other parent should have the opportunity to spend time with the children because after all the children are theirs.

Private Bills-Divorce
But with this background and having in mind the fact that in 1955 the father obtained a legal separation and custody of the children, none the less the evidence given to the Senate committee by the petitioner or father indicates, as shown on page 15, that one of the children, the daughter, has lived with her mother at times in New York, Montreal and Ste. Adele. Apparently the daughter moves back and forth from the father to the mother. Regardless of the legal position with respect to custody of the children, it would seem that this situation has existed for some time.
In this case there was also some discussion between the husband and the wife about a divorce. I intend to read the evidence to indicate precisely what the discussion was. I do not want to run afoul of the hon. member for Halifax and have him accuse me of selecting phrases and words out of the evidence in order to paint a particular picture. I suggest to him that in all fairness I have not attempted to do that on any occasion, and if the hon. member for Halifax is going to rise and suggest that is what I am doing in this case then my only alternative is to read all the evidence into the record, which will take considerably more time. There are two references with respect to the discussion about divorce. As found on page 14, Mr. Joyal, counsel for the petitioner, asked the petitioner questions about arrangements. He said:
Q. Did you make any arrangements with your wife so that she might give you evidence for the purpose of obtaining a divorce before this committee?
A. No. In 1956 she came back to Montreal, about four or five months after I found she was in Garden City. She came back and phoned me and wanted to meet me. She said that if I had no objections she was going to take divorce proceedings and I said, no, and she wanted to see a lawyer and apparently she did not go through with it.
Apparently the wife wanted to make some arrangements for a divorce but the husband said no, he did not want to have anything to do with it. Certain other evidence found on page 13 is probably connected with the desire on the part of the wife to obtain a divorce. About a third of the way down the page Senator Isnor asked this question:
Q. Who was the man? Were you given the name?
This was after the petitioner had indicated that he had found out that his wife was living with someone else. The petitioner replied:
A. His name was ... She was living with him at-
Then he gave the address in Garden City, Long Island.
About a year afterwards she was in the Lauren-tians and she came to my office and introduced this Mr.... to me. I thought that was a little odd.

He may have thought it a little odd but I think we are entitled to wonder whether or not this was also an indication on the part of the wife that she was desirous of getting a divorce, that she wanted to show him the particular person she was living with and perhaps indicate that everything would be all right one way or another if they could get a divorce.
Then there is the evidence of the investigators and again we have Mr. Charron who has acted in a number of these cases. His evidence is again stereotyped and it makes one wonder whether or not what he says happened is in fact all that occurred. Again I must say that I did not hear the remarks that the hon. member for Halifax made from his seat on the last occasion when these bills were being dealt with but in looking at Hansard I find that he inquired whether I never believed anyone who testified under oath. That is not the case at all, neither in this nor in any other instance. This is the evidence given by Mr. Charles Charron and he is bound by it. When one questions that evidence one is not saying that the evidence is incorrect or that Mr. Charron has perjured himself, but it may well be that the full story has not been told. There is often quite a difference between being told the complete story and only part of the story. Where the evidence is not clear, where there are incongruities or strange things seem to exist, we are entitled to wonder about these things and relate them to the other activities in the case. I do not know whether Mr. Joyal or the members of the Senate committee did not want to deal with these things. I think it is necessary to refer to the full examination by Mr. Joyal of Charles Charron, the investigator, and I read from the evidence:
Q. X show you exhibit 2 in this case, which is a photograph?
A. That is Mrs. ... That is the photograph I had at the time of the investigation.
Q. What investigation did you make with respect to her?
A. I got all the information from Mr. Hetu-
I am jumping to a conclusion here but I believe he was the lawyer who arranged the legal separation in 1955.
-that she was living in New York at... Garden City, Long Island, so I went there.
Q. What date?
A. On the 18th of February, 1959.
Q. What happened?
A. We went to ... about 8 o'clock in the morning-
When he says "we" he is talking about himself and his partner Mr. Morin. I continue:
A. We went to-about eight o'clock in the morning and at nine o'clock we saw a man come out and he went away. We stayed there and at 10.30 we saw a woman come out, Mrs.-the lady on that picture, and she went to a shopping centre not

far from there. She had her dinner at the shopping centre, in the restaurant, and came back home with some parcels at 2.30 in the afternoon, and at six at night we saw the same man who went out in the morning come in and at ten o'clock we saw the light go out and at 11.30 we went to the door and there was a big mailbox marked, "-" on the mailbox.
He refers to the name of the corespondent. I continue:
We rang the doorbell several times before the same man we saw going up there at six o'clock came and opened the door. We went in.
All the way in; there was no argument at this stage about asking who he was, or what his name was; he just went in. He went not only in through the door, but into the bedroom. He said:
We went to the bedroom on the left hand side and Mrs.-was lying in the bed, a full size bed. I went near the bed and said, "You are Mrs.-?". She said yes. I showed her the photograph and she admitted that it was a photograph taken of her. So I says to the man, "You are Mr.-?" And he admitted it and he says, "What's this for?" And I told him it was divorce proceedings that Mr.- was taking against his wife, so the man started to get mad and pushed us out and we went out.
Finally, after all of this the man started to get mad. This is very stereotyped sort of evidence that Mr. Charron is quite adept at giving. He seems to glory in it, after having discovered probably that this is the type of evidence that is necessary to meet the tests established by the other place with respect to divorce.
I point out again, if I may, Mr. Chairman, that here are two strangers, unknown to the respondent and the corespondent. Not only that, they are not in the same city and often not in the same country. They are in New York, in Garden City on Long Island, and at 11.30 in the evening after the lights have been out for an hour and a half-and I assume that if this couple were living together as man and wife, as the evidence would indicate they might well have been asleep by that time-this man rang the doorbell several times and a gentleman came to the door and opened it and the two strangers walked in. They walked into the bedroom and asked questions. They asked the lady in bed what was her name and to identify the picture. They got an admission from her as to who she was. Then the man started to get mad, after all this had taken place.
As I indicated before in another case, this might well happen in one instance, but I submit it is stretching coincidence a bit to assume that in every case that Mr. Charron gets involved in the self-same things occur. He goes to a door; he knocks on the door; someone opens it. He walks in to the apartment, the house, or whatever it is. He walks into the bedroom without being asked one question
Private Bills-Divorce by anybody. He inquires of whoever is in bed what is his or her name. He shows a photograph, and then suddenly the individual who opens the door starts to get a little mad. Perhaps I should express these doubts. I doubt very much whether Mr. Charron was telling the exact truth when he made that statement. The man might have got mad in one particular case, but I do not think you could stretch it to the point of saying that it was absolutely true in each case that Mr. Charron happens to be involved in. I doubt whether this is what occurs.
I submit also that the evidence given by the petitioner is not quite accurate. The wife came back to Montreal in 1956, and about four or five months after her husband discovered that she was in Garden City. She came back and said she wanted a divorce; she was going to take divorce proceedings if he had no objection. On another occasion she brought the gentleman with whom she was living, the corespondent in this case, to the petitioner and introduced him. I submit that in this case there was agreement. There is no argument. There is no contest, and she undoubtedly was not the least bit surprised, neither was the corespondent, when at 11.30 at night a couple of strangers came knocking on their door, walked into the bedroom and asked them what their names were, showed them photographs and then left. I submit there is quite a bit of understanding with respect to this particular case in so far as getting the evidence before the committee is concerned.
There is one other incident which makes one wonder, not about this particular subject matter of divorce but about another matter submitted in evidence. I do not want to put a construction upon someone's words to express what was not there or a thought that was not there, but a particular word or phrase is used which in some circles is taken to mean, not something dishonest particularly but the putting on of a show in order to obtain a certain thing. In some circles it is called a front. When someone puts on a bit of a front it leaves the impression that he is a pretty decent chap, and so on, or that he is using it to gain some other end. This is commonly referred to as a front. This gentleman used this, and I wonder whether it might not be the subject matter of some investigation. At page 13, Senator Isnor asked this question:
Q. Do you still support her?
A. No, I am not supporting her because in 1955, having to make a request to the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for a radio station, I wanted to put up a front in the Laurentian where I intended to establish a radio station, and I ordered a house built for her in Ste. Adele.

I do not know that there is anything wrong with that. The use oi that word would indicate that he wanted to leave an impression with the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that he was established in this particular area so that he might get a radio station. This might well require some investigation by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in order to find just how people happen to get radio stations, and whether it is necessary to put on a front to get them.
This is quite apart from adultery in the case itself. Because of the activities of this particular woman during the period of their marriage when they were living together; the husband coming home and finding someone else in his place; the wife being away for a few days and living with another gentleman, and so on, this might put a different complexion on the case. Apart from this, though, apart from the fact that it looks as if there were some arrangement, there was no surprise to the respondent and the corespondent to find someone knocking on their door at 11.30, and so on, and walking in and asking certain questions about divorce, I submit there is a great deal more to talk about than the conduct of the wife herself.

I thank the sponsor for that information. I think it excuses Mr. Joyal in some respects, in relation to his questions, as to which he might not otherwise be excused. But I am rather surprised that the legal counsel always get answers to the questions they ask. In this case in particular one


of the senators, namely Senator Isnor, asks a question in two separate instances and these questions are not answered. I checked back over some of the other cases in order to find out whether this had been an instance where the Hansard reporters did not get the answer or just did not follow it. I find that when this is done the Hansard reporter or the clerk who is taking down the verbatim report always puts at the end of the question a notation to the effect that an answer was made but it was indistinguishable to the clerk or the reporter. In this case, for instance we find the following questions asked by Senator Isnor:
Q. What do you mean by Montreal?-Where do you say your daughter is?
A. She is in Montreal living with her mother.
Q. How long did you live and cohabit together after your marriage?
A. How long?
This question, of course, is not answered. The question is re-asked:
Q. Roughly, how many years?
There is no answer to the question. We go on to page 13 of the evidence and we find that Senator Isnor again asks the question:
Q. Did she occupy the home you had built?
There is no answer. I am surprised that the senators, when they did not get answers to these questions did not pursue the questioning a little bit further.
There is something else about which I should like to inquire in connection with this matter. In this authority by W. Kent Power entitled "The Law of Divorce in Canada" I read on page 30 some of the statutory bars in general that would prohibit divorce. It states as follows:
The absolute statutory bars to the granting of a divorce are connivance, condonation and collusion. If the plaintiff is shown to be otherwise entitled to a divorce but the evidence establishes connivance, condonation or collusion the decree must be refused.
They refer to a case in Alberta of Emeny v. Emeny in 1929. I suggest that maybe we have here quite a few instances of enemy versus enemy and sometimes friend versus friend; but the indication would be that if it is a case of friend versus friend, probably no decree should be granted. The quotation continues:
As courts can act only upon evidence, the trial judge cannot refuse relief on the ground of an absolute bar unless the evidence is such as to satisfy him that the bar exists; a mere suspicion that it does is not enough.
Then at page 31 it goes on to state as follows:
In an undefended case, the limits of the trial judge's inquiry, either by constituting himself a cross-examining counsel or otherwise, must be left to him; and if the view be correct that there is a

provisional presumption against condonation, connivance and collusion it would seem that the better practice is for the judge himself to question the plaintiff on those points in the first place.
I think that indicates quite clearly that if the courts are handling these cases consideration is to be given to some of the constitutional bars. Because the courts are not hearing these particular cases I suggest it is the obligation of members of parliament to do the best they can in order to satisfy themselves that these statutory bars, as long as they are in our divorce act, are observed. I should like to read from the evidence as it was brought out by Mr. Joyal at page 12 where he starts his questioning:
Q. Are you living with her now?
A. No.
Q. When did you stop living with your wife?
A. September, 1949.
Q. You have not cohabited with her since?
A. No.
Q. Could you explain to the committee briefly what was the occasion that led to the separation in 1949?
A. Well, between 1940 and 1949 I was a singer and master of ceremonies for radio and nightclubs and I often had to go out of town to perform my contracts and when I came back home several times there was somebody else in my place. That is one of my reasons for the separation.
This may have been grounds for separation but it would not necessarily constitute grounds for a divorce unless he was willing to prove that adultery had taken place and also was willing to prove that not only had adultery taken place but that adultery had taken place which he had not condoned. The questioning continues as follows:
Q. Did this behaviour on the part of your wife continue over a long period of time? Was it something that was repeated?
A. Oh, yes. For a year and a half or two years after our marriage she kept going out late at night and even going off for a few days.
Q. But you continued to live with her nevertheless?
A. Yes, until 1949.
Q. And that is when you finally separated?
A. Yes.
Q. And you have been living separately and apart from each other since that tune?
A. Yes, since that time, September, 1949.
It would appear that during this time adultery was continually taking place. The questioning did not bring out the information as to with whom she had relations but it likely can be assumed that it was at least in some instances with the corespondent in this case. If this is true, it would indicate that condonation had taken place on a particular occasion. In other words, he had condoned this particular offence on a number of occasions and this would indicate that he had changed his mind and was not going to approve it after 1949, while at the same time he had done so for a number of years from 1940 to 1949.

This authority which I hold to be the leading one on divorce, at page 87 points out under "Discretionary Bars" in section 14, "Conduct Conducing to Adultery" as follows:
The wording of the act of 1857 (sec. 31) with respect to this discretionary bar is "such wilful neglect or misconduct as has conduced to the adultery". Such conduct must have been after the marriage. It has also been seen that, even when adultery, cruelty or desertion is set up as a reason for refusing the decree, the question whether it conduced to the defendant's adultery is a vital factor for consideration.
It goes on to point out that the court has to be very satisfied in a case of this nature as to what the wife's conduct was. Although it does not say this, it is indicated that the wife's conduct would come under common prostitution. Even if it was not the same person each time, we would at least be able to assume that she was promiscuous. It is pointed out that if this is the case then the judge must exercise a great deal of discretion in his own right. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in this case I would think this committee must exercise that right and decide whether it would be advantageous to the welfare of the state and the community in general to grant this particular divorce.
On page 73 there is reference to a discretion being exercised in favour of an adulterous wife although she has been living a life of prostitution. Mr. Justice Bucknill said:
The most difficult part of the case Is the fact that she continued to live in this way right on from 1928 to 1934, after she left her husband and at a time when she cannot say her husband was in any way forcing her to do this, or that he was in any way directly or indirectly responsible, except in this way, that he had, in my view, made it impossible for her to go back to him. He had failed to provide her with a proper home and failed to keep up the payments of 25 shillings a week which he had covenanted to do. That being so-

The law as such is quite clear about this. Condonation of a matrimonial offence means the forgiveness of the offence with full knowledge of the circumstances, followed by the reinstatement of the offending party to his

speechtext: In this case he points out that in 1940 when he was away he found someone was living at his home and he condoned it. I would suggest you cannot condone it for a period of time and then all of a sudden decide it is an offence. If you condone it once and there is a repetition-

speechtext: No. You can only have condonation after the offence.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: JOSEPH ALPHONSE YVES JEAN GABRIEL LALONDE
speechtext:
The hon. member knows more about it than I do, I am sure, and it is probably true that you can condone it once and forgive the party. Then next time you do it all over again. That may be true, but I suggest a period of nine years elapsed when this was the case and it was condoned over the whole of that period. Then he decides he wishes to get a divorce, and I suggest you cannot condone the same offence. There is no evidence which would indicate that it was not with the same person.
I suggest we should not accept the argument that adultery was being committed over these years, and that when it continued beyond the time it suited him that he has the right to say he is now going to object to it. Because it would indicate that he probably had established relationships elsewhere, and that he wanted a divorce rather than anything else.
In this treatise of what condonation involves the following is stated:
If a husband comes to one decision and means to act upon it, and then afterwards says, "Well, notwithstanding that I arrived at that decision and acted upon it, I am now going to take another line," it is clear that so far as a man is concerned, there is no going back.
In other words, if he condones an offence he has, in my opinion, to continue condoning it. If the wife got another boy friend I would suggest he might not be so happy to condone it as previously, but I think that is another line of thought altogether. I am sure we can legitimately pursue that line in this case, because he did not indicate that there was a different man with whom the wife was continuing to commit adultery from 1940 on. This treatise goes on:
One act of marital intercourse would always be construed as condonation. But in the case of a woman the courts have been far more lenient. The petitioner seems to have tried out the idea of returning to him, and having tried it out, altered her mind with the thought that perhaps after all she would like to go on with her proceedings.
This was in reference to a case where the lady had considered the divorce, as in this case, and then decided that the arrangements


were worthy of consideration and she decided not to go through with the divorce even though she had considered it for some time. Before I leave this I would like to refer to another part. It says:
Since condonation is a conditional forgiveness it must be distinguished from the irrevocable forgiveness conferred by a Rose v. Rose clause in a deed, or perhaps In a mere agreement supported by consideration whereby the parties covenant that no past offence shall be pleaded or admissible in evidence in any proceedings between them. What shall or shall not constitute condonation cannot be determined beforehand by agreement between the parties. Knowledge of the offence is essential to condonation and knowledge must be distinguished from suspicion. Therefore, condonation of an adultery of which the plaintiff was aware with one person does not condone adultery with another person of whom the plaintiff was not aware.
As will be seen from the evidence, there were a number of men involved in this case. Forgiveness of the offence is always complete forgiveness, and no further reference can be made to such an offence as far as the granting of a decree is concerned if the couple continue to live together. However, there may be some substance in what hon. members who are more learned in the law than I am have said, namely that each act of adultery may constitute grounds for a divorce decree. Therefore it might be possible that all the offences cannot be lumped together, as I would suggest they might; that any adultery committed would be grounds for divorce, and if it happened a hundred times it would be no different to it happening once. In this particular case application was made nine years after separation.
I am very unhappy about the fact that the Senate in dealing with the evidence in this case did not establish what the courts of Quebec had found with regard to the separation charge, because it would seem to me that if adultery had been charged and proved in Quebec we would not have too much difficulty about granting this divorce. I am concerned over the fact that the Senate has not given more consideration to the evidence as it was presented to a previous court. Since evidence with regard to the separation was admitted in the Senate, I think there was an obligation on the lawyer concerned to ask what the superior court of Quebec had done with regard to this separation. If a separation had been granted on an adultery charge, then the Quebec court would, of course, have taken into consideration the question of condonation with which we have been dealing. If they did not take that into consideration I think we should ask that this case be referred back to the committee until such time as inquiries have been made regarding the action taken by the superior court in Quebec in respect to it.

There is another point of law which does not seem to have played a large part in the determination of divorce cases in the past, and that is the question of delay. This couple ceased to live together. This probably happened, originally, in 1940, but the adultery at that time was forgiven. Adultery happened continually over the years, and then we find Mr. Charles Charron, a private investigator, going to another country and establishing an adultery charge which appears to differ in no way from the adultery charges that were continually being made over the years. This gentleman did not come to parliament and ask for a divorce until 1960. I presume, of course, that he started the case in 1959-

March 17, 1959. I would imagine that if we granted this application it would be a good St. Patrick's Day gift to the gentleman, if he is Irish. But that is an aside. We are concerned with this question of delay. This is a question which enters into these divorce cases in the same way, I presume, as it enters into other cases. It appears that the petitioner had not made up his mind as to what he wished to do. It may be outside our jurisdiction even to ask him what he has decided to do. However, there would seem to have been a great deal of delay between the date when a divorce was sought and the first occasion upon which one of these offences was committed, even if we take the 1949 date.
On page 82 of the Law of Divorce in Canada, section 11, under the heading "Delay", Mr. Power had this to say:
The delay which under the act ol 1857 (sec. 31) is a discretionary bar is "unreasonable delay in presenting or prosecuting the petition." The same discretion exists in New Brunswick and in Nova Scotia. The delay of the respondent in putting in a defence is a factor to be considered in deciding whether cross-relief asked for therein should be granted. The reason for the court frowning on delay was expressed thus by Sir Francis Jeune, in Johnson v. Johnson (1901) -
I read this only because many of us are not lawyers and do not have the advantage of the legal training which is necessary in order to handle legal cases. The citation goes on to give the reason put forward as follows:
The reasons why this court insists on steps being taken promptly, if they are taken at all, and why it should be very strenuous on the subject of delay, are that it is a terrible thing that people should be going about the world, neither married nor unmarried, possibly liable to contract fresh and illegal matrimony, and certainly exposed to temptation to commit adultery. This is a state of things which ought not to be prolonged for a moment longer than can be properly avoided.
The courts are very strict with regard to this matter of delay, and I think this is something to which we as a committee should give serious attention. Divorce cases have 79951-0-186

Mr. Chairman, there have been some thoughtful comments made in this debate. In particular, three legal points were raised, and perhaps some explanation should be given by myself as chairman of the committee.
With regard to the first point concerning condonation, I think the hon. member for Timiskaming fully answered his own question when he read excerpts from the authorities, the point being that one has to make up one's mind whether to forgive or not. The point is that you have to make up your mind whether or not you forgive. You can forgive a certain pattern of conduct and after a while if that pattern is continued while you cannot renege with respect to your original forgiveness you certainly do not have to forgive new offences that may occur from time to time. I believe that is the point here. The husband had forgiven everything that had occurred between 1940 and 1949 and after that he lost his patience to forgive.
With respect to collusion I gathered from the hon. members that there was no direct suggestion that there had been collusion. It was pointed out quite ably that the detectives had remarkably easy access into the home in New York. It was almost as though they had been welcomed there with open arms to obtain the evidence they needed for parliament. I think the point about collusion is this. If there had been an arrangement between the husband and wife and she were to go forth and commit adultery for the purpose of giving the husband evidence of adultery that would be clearly collusion and we should not entertain the petition here. If on the other hand she had set up a liaison with this man for some time-and it is pretty obvious in this case that that is what happened- and then made that evidence available rather easily to the husband that in the eyes of the law in such cases as Yaetes in Ontario and on the basis of other authorities would not be collusion. I believe that hon. gentlemen in the other place who heard this case as well as others observed the law very scrupulously and I would say it was applied very fairly in this case.
The third point raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming as to delay is a somewhat harder nut to crack. This would have been an excellent point if the hon. member had brought this newly acquired knowledge

Private Bills-Divorce of his before the committee so we could have had a greater examination of that particular point.

As I understand it, one of the major grounds on which the Quebec superior court grants legal separations is adultery. There is some reference in the civil code of that province to cruelty and other matters but legal separations are granted mainly on the grounds of adultery. If it is not possible for the province to apply adultery as a ground for other action it should indicate this in the cases that come before this house. When a separation is granted on the grounds of adultery in the Quebec superior court it should be proof of the grounds of adultery for divorce and we should no longer concern ourselves with it. That arrangement would speed up the processing of these cases.
I appreciate that complications may arise. As often happens a couple separated on the grounds of adultery may cohabit in the interval but if cohabitation does not occur after the separation is granted we should not concern ourselves with it any longer with respect to proof of adultery.

I had been saying that if these adjustments do not reflect the one year's study made by the pay research bureau

into the question of civil service salaries then we are entitled to draw the conclusion from the announcement of the minister that the wage increases were not in keeping with the recommendations made by the civil service commission to the minister some time ago. If they are not, and there is every indication on the surface that there is no connection between the $15 million announcement in the budget and the recommendations of the civil service commission, then I suggest that the pay research bureau, which is now conducting another one year study to be completed before the next budget is presented, is wasting its time if the minister is going to disregard the activities of that organization within the civil service commission which is supposed to deal with the question of civil service salaries.
But apart from all that I still think that a much more decent approach to the civil service salary structure and working conditions would be to grant bargaining rights to the employees within the public service. If the government has any real thought of putting into practice what it says it espouses, namely the competitive, free enterprise system, then it should certainly extend that concept of free enterprise to employees in the service of the government and allow the true and free play of competitive forces in collective bargaining to apply to the crown and to the employees in the public service. This is a proper extension of the theory in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) says he believes, and the free play of collective bargaining will be a most beneficial thing for civil servants, for the government service and for the government itself because it will have a tremendous effect upon bringing civil service salaries, which have been too low for so many years, into proper adjustment.
But I suspect that the government is afraid to do any such thing because it knows full well that it could not possibly justify its attitude on salaries for people in the public service before any type of impartial tribunal such as would have to be established if the civil servants had collective bargaining rights. In years past many private employers used to use precisely the same method as the Minister of Finance has used in order to weaken and destroy any effective growth of a union within a particular industry or among the employees of a particular employer. That is one reason why it is provided in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and in the various provincial labour acts that it is illegal for an employer to increase or decrease rates of pay and so on during a period of bargaining or during a period when a union is trying to become organized or certified.

This is an attempt on the part of the government to emulate the attitude that many employers used to have some years ago, an attempt to weaken the effect of any organization among its own employees. I do not intend to make any further comments at this time about civil service salaries or bargaining rights even though it may be upsetting to some hon. members opposite, especially those on the treasury benches.
One of the major features of the budget and the key to its nature is the use of the phrase, a balanced budget. I am quite sure that if the Minister of Finance applied the principle he has used to balance this budget to his own financial system within his household he would not think he was being fair to his family because certainly he would not want to limit his own personal financial arrangements to such an extent as to deprive his wife and children of food, clothing, shelter and things of that nature. But that is precisely what the Minister of Finance is doing with this balanced budget because on one side of the scale that functions in this balancing process there rest about 800,000 unemployed people. This is the balancing factor in the budget and nothing else.
I have here the figure of registrations at national employment service offices released on Wednesday, March 23, 1960, as at February 18, 1960. I do not say this is the latest figure that has been issued but it is the latest I have been able to obtain. I understand that the figure is higher since that time. However, it indicates that over 800,000 people are out of work in this country. Within the Pacific region alone, which comprises British Columbia primarily, there are more than 80,000 people out of work. It is a very unwise, unfair and discriminatory thing to balance a budget with 800,000 unemployed people.
While I am on the subject of the number of unemployed I would point out that there is, of course, some difference of opinion as to which set of figures should apply, those to which I have referred or the figures compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics. There is some question as to which set of figures is correct. Reference is often made to the national employment service statistics as to unemployed being incorrect because they reflect a number of people who in fact have jobs but are applying for other jobs and people who have secured work since registration. I point out that this is taken into account. In the publication to which I have referred there is a note at the bottom of table 2 reading in part as follows:
The count excludes registrations from persons known to have a job and applying for another one. Measures are also taken to exclude as far as possible persons who have secured work on their own since registration.

The Budget-Mr. Howard
Therefore these factors are taken into account. In addition to the number of unemployed registered with the national employment service offices, there is this factor which the footnote goes on to point out:
Not all persons who are looking for work register at N.E.S. offices.
That is quite true. In addition, there are a number of people who realize that they are not eligible for benefits, who have had a pretty sad experience with the national employment service so far as finding employment is concerned, and consequently they do not bother to register, or if they do register they do not bother to go back again once they find they are ineligible for benefits but rather attempt to find work on their own.
In addition to the 80,000 people who were out of work in British Columbia as of February 18 this year, there are an estimated 20,000 people not eligible for unemployment insurance who are on social welfare or municipal relief rolls.
Some time ago, in another debate-I believe it was the throne speech debate last year-I suggested that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) would be well advised to go out and stand in a bread line once in a while and find out what it feels like to stand in a bread line merely to get a sandwich because no work is available. I suggest it would do the minister a great deal of good to get much closer to the people who are unemployed and find out their problems rather than sit in his insulated plush office and continue to study and debate which set of figures should apply-

Mr. Speaker, you know full well that I always direct my remarks through you; I am doing that now. What I said was that it would do the Minister of Labour some good to go out and stand in a bread line and appreciate the views of the unemployed of this country. That is precisely what I said. The minister has been so engrossed in his facts and figures and fiction that it has not been possible for him to differentiate one from the other.
Unfortunately, while the Minister of Labour seems to stand the brunt of all the problems concerning the unemployed people in this nation, he is not the one to whom they should be directed because the Minister of Finance has far greater control over the cabinet than the Minister of Labour could ever hope to have. The Minister of Labour is the present head of the Department of Labour. The unemployment insurance commission comes under his direction, as does the national employment service. He issues the statistics. He argues as to which is correct and which is not. There is hope, because the minister has taken some action. If we want to be fair to the minister- unfortunately he is not here this evening; I am sure he will be apprised of what is said here in this debate-we must say that he has taken some action on this question of the unemployed. He set up a committee to attempt to resolve the differences of opinion between which set of figures is correct. This is an admirable approach because perhaps out of it all we shall finally get one set of statistics only to which the government may make reference, and they will be stuck with them. They will not then be able to take a set which incorrectly reflects the state of the unemployed, a low set, and say, "These are the ones which apply."
Unfortunately the committee which was established by the Minister of Labour was not received with too much revelry and rejoicing by the 800,000 people out of work. The establishment of the committee will not put them back to work. It will not feed their families; it will not provide them with employment; it will not pay their medical bills; it will not help to pay their portion of the national debt into which the Minister of Finance has driven them over the last couple of years. But it is something that the Minister of Labour has done.
It may well be, Mr. Speaker, that he has lost the program that he had a couple of

years ago. Perhaps he has lost the little sheets of paper he used to make reference to and say, "This is what we promised; this is what we will do." It may well be that that has been misplaced. If the minister does not have one of those promise sheets left, if he has destroyed or lost them, I would be quite happy to provide him with a copy so that the specific promises to the unemployed can be carried out.
I suggest that the real reason why the Minister of Labour is not, unfortunately, able to deal with this question, as he undoubtedly would like to, is that he is not able to propose the ideas that would bring about the solution. I think one of the reasons is that the Minister of Finance and others with him have too much say in the cabinet. The Minister of Finance is laughing at that, Mr. Speaker. Maybe he thinks he has not enough authority and wants more.
We all know there has been a shift in power in the cabinet. When this government was first formed there was speculation and hopes on the part of each cabinet minister as to who would be able to play his full part in government policy and whose ideas would be reflected in the government's decision on legislation when it was introduced. At least some of the hopes and ideas of the individual government ministers have been realized. Hopefuls have arisen from different parts of the nation, but I think the position has been pretty well solidified now. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) takes most of his counsel from ministers from the city of Toronto. The major person in this new emergence of authority behind the throne, of course, is the Minister of Finance, as he knows, and we know. The other is my very dear friend who is now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). He may laugh, but he is still the person who decides which part of the estimates is going to be slashed. First it is the Minister of Finance who decides, and then the Minister of Public Works puts the decision into effect. He slashes, he cuts the estimates and he discontinues the program that is supposed to be put into effect. He is the butcher of the estimates after he gets the order from the Minister of Finance. But they are doing the slicing in the wrong direction.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) comes from British Columbia. He, along with his associate minister, is the head of a department. If they want to go after it properly, if they want to use the knife and discontinue wasteful and foolish expenditures, here is the department in which to start. Do not start in the departments which mean so much to the individuals in this nation.

Unfortunately this power behind the throne, this desire to disregard completely the interests of the citizens of this nation, particularly the unemployed, the people we are talking about, leaves the Minister of Labour in an awkward position. His defence of the whole scheme must be to say to the opposition, "What do you want me to do?" This is what we have heard the Minister of Labour say so many times during this session. "What would you suggest; what would you do to overcome this problem?" We know full well he does not want any suggestions; he rejects them when they are given because the minister cannot be counted on to put them into effect, anyway.
If the minister requires any suggestions he will find there are lots of them; Hansard is full of them. The legislative assembly of British Columbia dealt with this question last year and made some recommendations about what the national government should do. All parties were represented on that committee in the legislature, as are committees in the house here. When I say all parties, I mean all parties that were represented in the legislative assembly itself.
We have a Social Credit government in British Columbia, as you probably know, Mr. Speaker, and that is bad enough without cluttering the house up with Conservatives. But the electorate in their wisdom decided they did not want any Conservatives in the legislature a few years ago. If we have an election this June some time, or May, or whenever it is that the premier of the province gets around to calling it, I am sure that when it is over there will not be any Conservatives in that parliament either.
Here is what the British Columbia legislative assembly recommended. This is not a partisan political document such as that which the Liberal party developed at its leadership convention a couple of years ago and that the C.C.F. necessarily would develop as its political platform. This is a report of a committee of the legislative assembly in the province of British Columbia. It is reported in the votes and proceedings of that legislative

The Budget-Mr. Howard assembly of Friday, March 20, 1959. In it this committee dealt extensively with unemployment and made recommendations as to what the national government could do, what the provincial government could do, the local government, the trade union movement and industry. It went rather thoroughly into the question of unemployment. It heard a great many representations. I will not read them all. They are listed in about one and three quarters pages. They include such companies as the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, which is certainly not a fly by night organization; the British Columbia Electric Company Limited; trade unions; the Canadian Legion; the fisheries association of British Columbia; Shuswap Okanagan Dairy Industry Company and Surrey Co-Operative Association. All of these organizations appeared and made representations to the committee and gave the committee the benefit of their ideas, beliefs and hopes in so far as the matter of dealing with unemployment is concerned.
I suggest that this procedure is what this government should have adopted earlier. It is still not too late to do so, but it should have been done earlier this session. Authority should have been given to the committee on industrial relations of this house to follow this course in order that the members of that committee might draw upon the wisdom of people outside of this parliament and outside of this government in respect of what action the national government should take on unemployment.
Let me read some references here as to the suggestions to the legislature in the province of British Columbia. As I say, I picked this example because it is the province from which I come-that is one reason-and because it cannot be charged-as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) or other cabinet ministers would like to charge, and as they have charged on other occasions

that the proposals advanced by members of the Liberal party or members of the C.C.F. party are nothing but political propaganda and do not mean anything, and that they are merely trying to get some free publicity or something of that nature. I therefore picked this example and here are the suggestions so far as the national government is concerned.

Then the next phase of this deals with the provincial government, the local government, and so on. However, I confine my remarks to those suggestions or recommendations by the select standing committee on labour of the legislative assembly of British Columbia contained in its report which appears in the votes and proceedings of March 20, 1959, just a bit over a year ago. Following its presentation I would assume that the report was communicated to the federal government or some cabinet ministers of the federal government, in order to draw these things to its attention as to what should be done about the matter by them.
The record of this government is fairly bad, even on these well worth-while suggestions that have been made here. Some of them have been done, certainly on a cooperative basis. As to the recommendation about forest access, transprovincial and interprovincial roads, we have some work proceeding on a trans-Canada highway but so far as transprovincial and interprovincial roads are concerned, the need for an expanded highway program which would provide employment and develop highway construction, we have nothing. We have the trans-Canada highway and the roads to resources. We have had an indication that something might be done later on. I am concerned about this "later on". It is our opinion that these are things that should have been planned some time ago, to be put into effect when they were most needed and in order to develop these roads on a sensible

basis instead of maybe a couple of years from now coming up with a scheme to do something of this nature.
As to park and camp site improvement, there has been some of this activity. As to diking and drainage projects, there is an extensive study which was made under the water resources branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources; by the Fraser river board dealing with diking and draining that is necessary along the lower regions of the Fraser river and certain other hydro projects further on north. That report is in the hands of the government. The government has had it since last year some time and it is sitting on it. The recommendations are there as to what could be done.
As to stream clearance projects and the creation of artificial spawning areas, we all know of what value fish is to British Columbia and of the need for employment in that regard. The flood control provisions on the Fraser river also are connected with the diking and drainage projects which have been thoroughly studied and reported on by the Fraser river board under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
As to the other suggestions made, there is the one with respect to the encouragement and promotion of the construction of coastal shipping. What we have is not an expansion of that industry but a reversal of that recommendation and a diminution of shipping facilities on the west coast.
As to research programs designed to encourage the use of coal and coal by-products, that recommendation applies not only to British Columbia but, as was pointed out by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) earlier today, it applies extensively to the maritime provinces. There is great need there for some machinery by means of which to make sure that our coal resources just do not sit idle and that coal miners are employed, and that we make some use of these natural resources.
Trade is another phase of this report. It deals with the republic of red China, and I appreciate the government's reluctance to do anything like that because of its fear of the United States.
There is the suggestion about provision of the ways and means to extend low cost credit. Instead of that occurring the finance minister has driven credit higher, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) is part and parcel of it in pushing up interest rates.
As to the recommendation to assist and encourage the establishment and growth of local industries, this is a prime thing that this government could do. The hon. member
The Budget-Mr. Howard for York-Sunbury again this afternoon made reference to the need for such industries to be established in the maritimes. The maritimes are not the only part of Canada that needs the insurance of some governmental agency to bring into their areas industries which will grow up and rise in an area to the end that long term full year employment can be obtained by the people in that area where there is none at the moment and where they are economically in a collapsed position or where there is one industry and any shift in the economy of that particular industry upsets the working force and upsets the economy of the whole area around there.
I suggest that this national government on the question of developing industries should, if necessary, underwrite the capital expense involved. It should provide a reserve or a revolving pool or fund which could be loaned out on a selective basis. It would have to be on a selective basis because we have not the resources to lend money toward the entire capital expansion needs of Canada. This money should be loaned out either at a low interest rate, or at no interest rate at all if that is necessary to ensure the growth of an industry. These concessions should be provided in order that industry could go into places on a planned basis-not a haphazard basis but a planned, co-ordinated basis-to ensure the best possible supply of employment opportunities.
But the government does not want to do anything about that at all. It has that philosophy that the blind progress of our economy will eventually work itself out. We have depressions, recessions or lay-offs. We have three quarters of a million people unemployed every winter, so apparently this is no minor detail. It is part of the necessities of having this so-called free enterprise economy, which incidentally in its true sense we do not have. But because the government has this philosophy, these are the problems resulting from it: unemployment, declining trade and declining production. The government cannot cope with this particular problem if it continues to act like an ostrich and stick its head in the sand every time something dangerous occurs, and then while it has its head in the sand and its eyes and ears covered, hopes that the problem will straighten itself out.
A budget which, as I said, has on the one hand more than three quarters of a million unemployed people in Canada as the balancing factor, and a budget which continually talks about prosperity just around the corner, is not worthy of the name of a budget and should not receive the support of hon. members of this house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great pleasure to have the opportunity of taking part in the budget debate on behalf of my constituents of Waterloo North. Our Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), a man of outstanding ability and sincerity, is to be congratulated for his splendid presentation and the terrific amount of work he has contributed to the preparation of this budget. Every hon. member of this house will appreciate his untiring efforts and loyalty in carrying out his important duties as Minister of Finance.
Through the kindness of our esteemed Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and yourself, Mr. Speaker, I was chosen as one of the delegates, along with four fine gentlemen, to represent parliament in West Germany as guests of that government last September. Perhaps one of the most impressive events was the inauguration of the new president, Dr. Lubke, who succeeded Dr. Heuss, beloved by the German people. This took place in the city of Bonn, the present seat of the West German government. Dr. Gestemeir, the speaker, in his opening remarks made mention of our presence. His words drew real applause from all those present. The hospitality of the German people was excellent, and I feel that our good will tour was of great benefit to both countries and will help establish better trade relations.
Mr. Speaker, your leadership of this delegation demonstrated your personal cordiality and sincerity as well as a deep understanding of the problems confronting us in our daily obligations. May the divine benediction rest upon you as you guide us in our duties for the strengthening of our great nation and the promotion of the public good.
May I as a member of the House of Commons observe that we have a busy schedule ahead according to the budget speech. The issues we will debate are of the utmost importance to the future of Canada. One of them that touches the heart of my industry-packed constituency of Waterloo North is the discussion of our international trade that will be carried on in this house. I hope that when international trade is discussed we will examine closely the effect that imports from low-wage countries are having on our Canadian industries, industries that have grown up with Canada and which have placed all their money, their hope and, yes, their trust, in the future of Canada.
The impact on the Canadian rubber industry of imports from low-wage countries, especially Japan and Hong Kong, has long been known. It has been pointed out before in this house during the Liberal administration but to no avail. It has caused serious

harm to rubber footwear industries in my constituency of Waterloo North and in other parts of Canada. However, other industries have also been hard hit by these imports, such as the radio, television, button and shirt manufacturing industries. Again they make up important segments of the industry of my constituency. It has been pointed out to me that two years ago only 10 per cent of all radios sold in Canada were imported. Today that figure is between 40 and 50 per cent. That has meant a loss in volume to one Kitchener manufacturer of approximately 30,000 small table radios alone.
Two of the largest shirt manufacturers in Canada, along with smaller firms, employing about 2,000 people are also situated in my constituency. They, too, are asking for some government help.
Concerning tariff changes, we are informed that an important round of tariff negotiations under GATT will be initiated this autumn. Many proposed tariff changes may find some place in the forthcoming negotiations.
Turning to the rubber footwear industry in Canada, the latest figures for the 11 month period in 1959 as compared to the same period in 1958 shows that the percentage of the total consumption of waterproof footwear imported into Canada increased from 17.6 per cent during the 1958 11 month period to 31 per cent in the same period in 1959. In canvas footwear the percentage jumped from 58.9 per cent in 1958 to 68.5 per cent in the same 11 month period in 1959. To sum it all up, in the first 11 months of 1959 approximately 46 per cent of the total consumption of waterproof and canvas footwear was imported.
I realize the tenuous position that the government holds because of this country's trade position, especially with Japan, the country from which much of these imports are coming. I realize, too, that in order to keep exporting-especially wheat-to Japan we must buy in return a good amount of Japanese products. I know our government is very anxious to help solve this problem. Let us therefore use every effort in finding a way to maintain trade with Japan, but at the same time see that our Canadian industries that have grown up with Canada, that have placed all their money, their hope, and yes their trust, in the future of Canada are able to flourish and continue to provide employment for thousands of our Canadian citizens.
Just a word about our federal civil servants. As a former civil servant for more than 35 pears, and knowing some of their problems I was pleased to hear in the budget address that treasury board had approved

recommendations from the civil service commission involving some 50,000 employees of the public service. May I suggest that consideration be given to revising salaries in the under $6,000 bracket as soon as possible, and that also serious consideration be given to salary increases for our armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
A few months ago, the Kitchener-Waterloo Dutchmen of my Waterloo North constituency represented Canada in the Olympic hockey championship at Squaw Valley, California, winning the silver medal. Like many Canadians, I was disappointed in the final result. However, as a sportsman and lover of wholesome recreation I felt justly proud of their achievements. Their supreme effort was not quite good enough to win the gold medal for Canada, but their gentlemanly conduct and good sportsmanship rated them as top-ranking good-will ambassadors for Canada.
Many sportswriters and sportcasters, along with individuals, have spent much time in finding a formula to provide better conditions for our competing athletes in Olympic competition. What is the answer? May I suggest two points that may be of some assistance to this question? It is my firm belief that schools in every province, not only to cover hockey but all recreation, could be started about four months before the beginning of the Olympic games, provincial governments to provide the financial assistance. Through the efforts of these schools the top athletes could be chosen to represent Canada.
My second thought concerns the federal government and the acceptance of the resolution as proposed by one of the hon. members from Vancouver on the subject of a Canada sports council, with the financial assistance coming from our government to defray expenses of our competing Canadians. This council, representing every province, could provide the necessary assistance and inspire our youth to take a greater interest in Canada's Olympic team. The outcome of such efforts could be the greatest enemy of juvenile delinquency.
Let us face the facts, especially with regard to hockey, Canada's national game. We have taught this sport to other countries, and in most cases they have been good scholars. The competition has become tougher, and in order to compete successfully our government, along with provincial governments, assisted by athletic associations all across Canada, must lead the way.
As a veteran of the first great war I am naturally intensely interested in the welfare of those who lost dear ones; disabled veterans, and all veterans and their dependents. I know it is not necessary for me to remind our government to give further consideration to their
The Budget-Mr. Weichel requests for pension increases and other assistance. Their sacrifices and services have been deeply appreciated by our government, the Canadian people and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks). Their needs, financial and otherwise, should continue to be one of our first obligations.
About a year ago I mentioned in this house the possibility of a university in the city of Waterloo, Ontario. Since that time, this has become a reality. The value of education is becoming more important daily, and I would like to congratulate the member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) for her recent remarks on this subject. The Waterloo university college board of governors decided recently in favour of federating with the university of Waterloo. The faculty of St. Jerome's College had previously made such a decision. In the very near future agreements to federate will be signed by both church colleges with the university. The federation program will become effective July 1, 1960.
Enrolment at Waterloo college had grown in the last six years from 168 full-time arts students to over 500 this year. The university enrolled its first students in July 1957, and the students now enrolled in its co-operative engineering course total over 600. When the two related church colleges come into federation with the university the total enrolment will be between 1,200 and 1,300 students. In addition, the university is serving the community through its adult education program which has an enrolment in excess of 1,000 people.
On the university's new campus of approximately 200 acres there are now two large buildings completed and in use, the chemistry and chemical engineering building, of 54,000 square feet, and the physics and mathematics building of 100,000 square feet. Dr. Steacie, head of the national research council, officially opened the physics building on February 10 last. The total faculty of the university and colleges numbers over 100. Architects are now developing plans for the university's engineering building which is scheduled for completion in 1962. In addition to the Lutheran and Roman Catholic churches operating Waterloo University College and St. Jerome's respectively, the Anglican church and the Mennonites have also indicated an interest in building residences on the university campus for the use of the students of their denomination who are attending the university.
Only a short time ago the university publicly announced the appointment of its chancellor, the Hon. Dana Porter, chief justice of the supreme court of Ontario. As you are aware,

The Budget-Mr. Weichel his lordship is a man who is highly regarded for his public service, especially in the field of education. The fact that Hon. Leslie Frost encouraged Mr. Porter to accept the appointment is an indication of the high esteem in which the university is held by the premier of this province. The Kitchener-Water loo Record of January 8 rightly states, and I quote:
It is important that all those involved in this great development should resolve to devote their efforts to its creative exploitation.
