Last spring I spoke briefly to this house in favour of new federal plans for emergency measures and civil defence which had been announced a few weeks previously by the Prime Minister. At this time I want to add that the progress and development since last spring have justified the optimism I expresed then as to the workability of the new plans made, thanks to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) and others.
Since then the ten provinces again met with the federal emergency measures ministers and officials at Ottawa early in October, after the provinces had had an opportunity of studying for some months the new realignment of duties and responsibilities between the federal government agencies, including the army, the provinces and municipalities. All the press reports since have indicated a remarkable unity of acceptance by all provinces of the new proposals as being both feasible and acceptable.
These emergency measures are the civilian counterpart of the Department of National Defence and the armed services with respect to what has to be done to protect the civilian population and their governments and operations in the event of war.
I am sure that all hon. members of this house will join with me in the hope that such

measures may never be needed, and that the release of world tension which has occurred during the interchange of visits between the leaders of the world powers will continue and grow. But until the world does come to true disarmament, these emergency measures for the protection of our civil population are indeed necessary.
Just so long as this parliament finds it necessary to vote many millions of dollars for the armed services and to maintain radar lines across Canada to give warnings of enemy attack and to develop missile bases in Canada, just so long will it be equally necessary for this government to expend funds and carry out planning in emergency measures and in civil defence to protect our civilian populace.
From all the reports I have heard the progress across Canada in the new realignment of responsibilities and duties has been both substantial and satisfactory. In particular, I want to commend the Canadian army for the realistic way it has taken hold of its new responsibility to carry the warning of any enemy attack to the people across Canada and to assume the battlefield command of the rescue and other forces which would have to act in areas which have been damaged by enemy bombing or heavy fall-out of radioactive dust. In not only the regular army but also in all their militia units this program which was begun only eight months ago is now proceeding with dispatch under the able and energetic leadership of the general officer commanding of the central region.
Some time ago the provincial government in my own province of Ontario took formal action so that it too could co-operate fully with the federal government and the army in these emergency measures for the continuity of government and the survival of our people in the event of enemy attack. On January 14, 1960, under order in council 201/60 the province of Ontario established an emergency measures organization for Ontario to parallel and co-operate with the federal emergency organization. The provincial organization includes various provincial government departments whose continued functioning would be immediately necessary in the event of enemy attack, and whose functioning is limited to carrying out the provincial responsibilities under this new alignment.
The new Ontario organization remains within the ministerial direction of Hon. W. M. Nickle, Q.C., minister of planning and developing, who has been charged with heading the old civil defence branch, while the chairman appointed by order in council is Mr. W. J. Scott, Ontario fire marshal, whose county fire mutual aid organization throughout the province is accepted as a pattern

for the fire defence organization across Canada, and who is well known for his work in civil defence over a long period of time. His contribution to civil defence has been outstanding. *
In my own riding of Waterloo North we have had within recent months three cases where the automatic assistance of all the fire departments in the county of Waterloo was immediately available under this organized emergency mutual fire aid program. Undoubtedly, in all instances this county organization in Waterloo county saved hundreds of thousands of dollars of potential fire loss. They are peacetime examples of the value of organizing now for any emergency that may occur in either peace or war. This is what I feel the new emergency measures organizations are geared to do in all three of the municipal, provincial and federal levels of government. Our government is to be congratulated for its splendid progress in civil defence.

Mr. Speaker, the budget which was presented before this house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) last Thursday generally was termed as a stand-pat, an unexciting budget. Unexciting it may have been to the ones who were not deprived of the necessary things of life in the course of the past year, to the ones who were able to make both ends meet in providing for their families the food, clothing, medical care and educational facilities required. When there is the assurance that these same opportunities will again be provided this budget might very well be considered, indeed, a satisfactory budget. But to those others who have seen the necessities of life evade them, to those whose incomes have left them wanting in their ability to provide to their families those things necessary to their physical and educational welfare, to those hundreds of thousands presently unemployed, this is not a satisfactory budget. On the contrary, it is a barren and gloomy budget and the bringer of gloom is the Minister of Finance.
The expected increase of 6 per cent in the gross national product alone cannot fill the gap in providing sufficient employment outlets to all those Canadians in need of income at the present time. Too much stress is also being laid again on statistical data in the present budget while forgetting the humanitarian aspect in terms of those in the country who are being denied what is a fundamental right of every citizen, namely the right, when willing to work, to earn a fair living for himself and for his dependents. It is with a sense of deep responsibility that
The Budget-Mr. Michaud I contend that the most urgent national problem, namely unemployment, was ignored or conjured away by the minister in the presentation of his last budget.
It is noted that a broader interest is manifested these days in the economic problems of the maritime provinces particularly. Here is a situation which calls for a broad national recognition if it is to be resolved. As a representative of the maritime provinces in this parliament I feel it is my duty at this time to deal with some aspects of the faltering economy of those provinces even at the risk of reproof and rebuff by some other representatives from that area whose utterances in this house since the opening of the present session would tend to indicate that all is well in the maritimes, that the maritimes are going through a period of great boom at the present time.
A week ago I returned to Ottawa following a few days' visit in my constituency. The conditions I found there are simply disheartening. I do not wish to be considered an alarmist or pessimist but I am saying that the conditions there are the worst we have had since the great depression in the early 1930's. If it were not for those social benefits introduced by Liberal governments which are paid every month such as old age assistance, old age pensions, family allowances and unemployment insurance-to those who are fortunate enough not to be denied unemployment insurance through vexatious interference in the application of the law-if it were not for these different forms of social assistance I say that conditions there would be, if not worse, at least in every way as bad as they were in the early 1930's.
Surely this is a situation which deserves more sympathetic attention than mere lip service when we realize that the main source of income in some parts of the maritime provinces at the present time is under the form of social benefits in one way or another. It was stated recently that about 20 per cent of the labour force in the province of New Brunswick was unemployed. That being the case, I feel that the percentage in some particular areas of that province is well over one third of the labour force. Do we realize all the social implications in a community plagued with such depressed conditions?
How long can we remain indifferent to the needs of such a sizeable segment of our population in a country where we speak of high standards of living, of notable economic expansion and high social development? We often speak of immigration in this house. I am not against immigration but I do contend that if our economy permits the integration every year of thousands of immigrants

The Budget-Mr. Michaud then we should also be able to take care of those Canadian born citizens who are destitute and in every way as much in need of a steady means of livelihood.
The morning I left home to return to Ottawa last week I paid a visit to the office of a local lawyer who told me that his main occupation during the past winter months had been preparing visas for people emigrating to the United States. That same morning he had had four new applications, and this lawyer is only one of those engaged in that same business at the present time. Can we not logically contend that such a situation is inadmissible?
What is going to happen to the economic and social structures of our municipalities if this mass exodus of our people to another land in quest of a situation which will procure them a livelihood continues? These municipalities at one time or another have contracted certain obligations toward these people with the expectation that the greater part of the population would normally remain in their midst. For instance, who is going to remain responsible for the school debentures of these municipalities if too great a number of these young people for whom these schools were built have to leave the municipalities and the country? No municipality can afford to provide educational facilities to a whole generation for the benefit of another country. In this respect alone we could end up in a very embarrassing situation.
Does it mean that no solution can be devised to remedy such an abnormal situation? Surely we have not reached a point of such utter defeatism where we must admit that ways and means cannot be devised to remedy such depressed conditions. Indeed, concrete suggestions have been and still are being made in the face of the public awakening to the necessity of an economic revival in the maritime provinces. Foremost, there is the necessity for the whole country to realize that this is a national emergency. In this respect I can do no better than to quote the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who, in dealing with this problem, had this to say as found at page 1693 of Hansard of March 3, 1960:
There is something else we have to accept. The wealthier parts of this country will have to accept obligations, perhaps in the way they have not in the past, to the economically weaker and less developed parts of the country and to help solve their special problems. There is only one way it can be done. And it has been done in the United Kingdom. If you read the United Kingdom program for the depressed areas you will see how it was done. Nor did they have the financial and economic resources over there at that time that we have in this country now. The only way it can be done is by government schemes of capital assistance to encourage industrial and economic redevelopment


in those areas. Perhaps this redevelopment aspect of the problem is as important as new development projects in our economy. If that should mean -and I suppose it would-heavier tax burdens, no Canadian has the right to complain if the taxes, if the money from those taxes, is used to put into effect constructive and forward-looking plans worked out in co-operation with the provinces so that we will not have underdeveloped areas in this country indefinitely in the future. I am thinking, of course, particularly of the Atlantic provinces.
This assistance could take the form principally of major capital works projects. This form of assistance has already been available in the maritimes to the great benefit of all. I had the occasion to mention in another debate last year that at one time anyone who wanted a job in the maritimes could get it when construction was under way at Camp Gagetown and at the airfield bases in the Labrador region. These projects are now mostly completed and alternate projects have not been initiated, accounting in part, therefore, for the heavy backlog of unemployed in the maritimes at the present time.
But other major projects are needed in the maritimes. Foremost is the construction of the Chignecto canal, which has aroused the interest of the maritime provinces as a whole recently. There is the construction of a causeway between Prince Edward Island and the New Brunswick mainland. There are those other numerous industrial developments promoted by APEC, a council formed to promote the economy of the Atlantic provinces and which is engaging the minds of all the civic-minded leaders of the Atlantic provinces. It is, therefore, the responsibility of the present government in consultation with the Atlantic provinces authorities to seek ways and means whereby appropriate and adequate measures can be devised to revive the general economy of the Atlantic provinces. Then it will be the duty of the government to act.
While it is urgent that we devise such a program of capital works, nevertheless great attention should also be given to achieve the greatest development possible of our primary industries. There is room, I submit, for broad improvements in this respect. The three main industries in the Atlantic provinces are farming, lumbering and fishing. Of these three basic industries, agriculture remains to the forefront if considered in its social as well as its economic aspects. A sound agricultural community reflects an element of stability and balance in the framework of the nation at large.
The question arises today as to how long the farm community will be able to subsist in the face of the difficulties besetting that industry. In a general economy of expansion and growth in the country agriculture

finds itself in this unhappy cost-price squeeze position which, if allowed to persist much longer, might jeopardize the whole stability of the industry. Indeed, how much longer can farmers subsist if on the one hand the prices they receive for the goods they sell are continuously going down while on the other hand the prices they have to pay for the goods and services they have to buy are going up? Farmers in the Atlantic provinces and in my own riding are, therefore, anxiously waiting to see what the present government will have to offer to solve this crucial problem.
Farmers are also waiting to see what is going to happen to the deficiency payment policy on eggs and hogs which has brought such unsatisfactory results up to this time. I was told that since the inception of this inept law last January hogs have sold in the maritimes for as low as 18 cents a pound, never reaching a higher point than 23 cents a pound, which is under the 23.5 cent support price. Since the deficiency payment on pork is to be calculated on a yearly national average it might very well happen that if prices go up toward the latter part of the year, due to a scarcity brought about by many farmers being forced out of hog production, then those who have been selling at 18 and 19 cents may never recuperate any differential price at all. Unless an offer to purchase by the government is re-established in pork marketings the industry will be faced with a situation which could have ruinous consequences.
Farmers are also anxiously awaiting the introduction of the newly formed farm credit corporation. Many farmers in the Atlantic provinces are anxious to increase their holdings, but wonder whether the new government credit agency, the farm credit corporation, will operate with more flexibility than the former farm loan board. I feel very strongly that drastic measures will have to be adopted if we wish to see agriculture in the maritime provinces regain the stability it needs to restore confidence in the industry.
The fishery is also an important segment of our economy in the Atlantic provinces. Great strides have to be made in the industry if we wish to ensure a fair standard of living to those engaged in that way of life. To get a fair estimation of the general situation of some fishermen along the eastern shores, one has only to remember something that was pointed out that at the time of the Escuminac disaster last June, that is that the average income of those who were the victims of that storm-there were some 35 of them-was between $600 and $700 a year. It is very hard to realize how anyone can eke
The Budget-Mr. Michaud out a living for himself and his family with such an income. Yet many of our local fishermen are within that category. Of necessity, something must be done to supplement the income of those low income fishermen if they are to enjoy a fair share of the national income.
When we analyse the situation we find that many of these people, while engaged in fishery for part of the year only, are living on land holdings of some considerable size. This land, in almost every case, while fertile, tillable land which could produce many of the things needed for the fishermen's families, is left in complete abandonment. It is true that certain capital, now not within the reach of the ordinary fisherman, would be required to carry on a supplementary farm operation, somewhat of a sideline operation. That is where I submit a fisherman's fund, something along the lines of the farm credit corporation, and in conformity with the nature of the enterprise, should be established. It would permit those fishermen with insufficient income and who hold some farm land to carry on small farm operations proportionate to their family needs.
Incidentally, the history of most of those fishing settlements along the shores would indicate that in most cases they were founded primarily on an agricultural basis. It was only when fishing became an important industry that farming in those areas was abandoned. Circumstances today would justify a return to the former practice of conducting farming and fishing operations concurrently, where fishing alone is insufficient to bring adequate returns to ensure the livelihood of the fisherman's family. I therefore submit the above recommendations to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) who I know is anxious to do everything possible to help the rehabilitation of those submarginal fishermen.
In another respect I wish to make certain recommendations concerning the protective measures of our fisheries, of the lobster fishery in my part of the maritimes particularly. I am happy to say that some measure of success has been encountered in this respect since last year. The great majority of our lobster fishermen now realize the importance of returning to the sea undersized and berried lobsters to ensure a continuous lobster catch from year to year. Unfortunately there are still those who, unscrupulously, fail to obey the law, thus causing great prejudice to themselves and to all those others who are cautious enough to respect the law. I realize how difficult it is for the protection officers to cope with every case in this respect. But I wish to reiterate that the great majority of

The Budget-Mr. Michaud the lobster fishermen want the full enforcement of those protective measures. I urge the department, through its protective staff and officers, to continue its efforts in this respect until it has succeeded in stopping all those guilty of those wrongful poaching practices. The lobster industry is a valuable one along the Atlantic sea coast. It is often referred to as a little gold mine. Let us make sure that we keep that industry at its highest state of production from year to year. We need that industry.
Our third primary industry in the mari-times, and in my own constituency as well, is the lumber industry. Here again is a field where the returns are not commensurate with the value of the product and the cost to produce it, thus showing a detrimental effect on the economy of that particular industry. As an example, pulpwood, which only a few years ago was selling at $17 a cord is now selling at $10 a cord. Little wonder, therefore, that farmers had to reduce their cuttings on their own woodlots. Farmers cannot afford to hire woodsmen to produce wood for the market at such a depressed price. Many hands who formerly were occupied in that idustry are therefore left idle.
Would it not seem here again that wood prices should be brought more in line with the commodities bought with the returns of that product itself? After all, it is no secret that the price of those finished products coming from the processing of wood, pratic-ularly paper, has been rising steadily, while the price of wood has been steadily going down. The cost-price squeeze here again is having an unfavourable impact upon the economy of the industry. Until and unless conditions are regularized in this segment of the economy unemployment will continue to prevail in the lumber industry. It is, therefore, the responsibility of the government to create better conditions which will restore to this industry its former prosperity.
These are some of the recommendations which I deemed it advisable to make to the government in this budget debate concerning the general economy of the maritime provinces and the economy of my riding. I have tried to make these objectively, with the hope that it might cause the government to give its attention to the crucial problems with which we are so greatly concerned at the present time.
Before concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, there is another matter with which I should like to deal briefly. I have in mind certain aspects of the administration of the unemployment insurance commission. At the outset, let me emphasize the fact that my remarks at this time are not directed at any

officials in any particular office but rather at the policy of the commission itself.
In the maritimes we have a larger number of unemployed people than in any other part of the country, proportionately speaking. This is a situation imposed upon us by circumstances over which we have no control. I say this because I have an impression, at times, that there are some who like to refer to that situation disparagingly, as if we in the maritimes carried the responsibility for that situation. Lest there be any misapprehension in this respect let me emphasize the fact that our workers in the maritimes are as capable, as industrious and as eager to work as are their fellow workers in other parts of the country. If there is any difference between the status of our workers and that of the workers of other regions it is not in their character but in their opportunities to find employment.
I feel that this situation is often abused at the expense of the maritime workers, both by the employers and by the commission in its decisions to allow benefit warrants. I do not wish at this time to defend the case of those who, at times, attempt to qualify themselves through irregular methods. These, of course, must be repelled. But too often applicants of good will, with good cases, are penalized through vexatious interference devices which should not be tolerated.
Too many woods employers, for instance, during winter months particularly wish to take advantage of the law governing the commission in order to impel woodsmen to perform certain jobs on a cord basis in nearly impossible conditions, just because they know that these woodsmen cannot refuse to go lest their unemployment insurance benefits be cancelled.
I know of a case during the winter of 1959 where scores of claimants were disqualified from insurance benefits just because they refused to work for a certain contractor who did not even have a real assignment to offer to those who reported for work. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) the other day referred to a case in which a claimant was refused unemployment insurance benefits because he refused to buy a $200 chain saw for a job which was guaranteed for only six weeks. I know of a worse case than that. On the job to which I referred just a moment ago I know of a man living 25 miles away who reported for work and who, upon finding there was no camp in which to stay, returned home, only later to have his unemployment insurance benefits cancelled because he did not accept work. In this instance I suppose he was expected to procure for himself an automobile

in order to cover daily the distance between the site of the job and his home since there was no other means of communication. I submit that cases such as these are cases of pure discrimination against the workers.
Then there are other happenings which occurred this winter where miscalculations are taking place and the claimants are then requested to reimburse the amounts they supposedly were not entitled to receive. How could we be more unrealistic than to expect workers, living on an income provided by unemployment insurance benefits for weeks and months, to reimburse that same money? Where do we suppose the money is going to come from?
It is a well-known fact that the unemployment insurance fund is now seriously depleted. But I cannot conceive of any reason why Canadian workers, especially the maritime workers, should be asked to compensate for a situation which is due to no fault of their own but rather to the mismanagement of a government which has spoiled the golden heritage bequeathed to it by a previous administration. The unemployment insurance commission in many ways should show better judgment in many of its dealings with Canadian workers whom it is supposed to protect and to assist and not to penalize indiscriminately.

Mr. Speaker, I should not miss this opportunity of extending my heartfelt congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for the greatness of his accomplishment in bringing down a surplus budget this year. Knowing what administrative difficulties he had to face when he took over the finance portfolio in 1957 and knowing also that he had to face a deficit of almost $600 million in 1958 and another deficit of $400 million in 1959, we are all amazed that he was able to bring down a balanced budget this year.
So, since the Conservatives have taken over, at a time when the whole country was worried, the Minister of Finance has succeeded with sheer perseverance and, above all, confidence in our national potentialities, to bring this country out of the doldrums prevailing under the previous administration and along the steady road to prosperity.
Today, the ordinary citizen when asked his opinion on the present budget, answers: "Things are better, keep it up".
In spite of all the sophisms and all the nonsense spread by the members of the opposition through all the publicity mediums at
The Budget-Mr. Bourbonnais their disposal, radio, press, etc., the average citizen, the farmer, the worker, finds out that we narrowly avoided a depression, through the feat of strength of the present government. Today, confidence is rising with the Conservative party, as revealed by the Gallup polls.
Besides, that is what prompts the outbursts of demagogy of our opponents who, instead of remaining calm and respectful in this house, spend their time laughing, getting excited, and jumping for no reason at all, and attempt to make light of all the suggestions made by the government.
For instance, when we took up the legislation to settle the problem regarding our universities a number of opposition members cracked jokes and tried to make fun of a problem which is so significant for the province of Quebec. In fact, I shall come back to that later on.
Mr. Speaker, before going on with my remarks, I would like, on behalf of all those I represent here, and also of those who did not have the opportunity to do so in the house, most sincerely to commend the hon. Minister of Finance for his delicate attention to the French speaking people of Canada, when he started his budget speech in French with an accent comparable to that of Her Gracious Majesty the Queen of Canada, when she addressed us in that language. There you have a positive action clearly indicating that, under this government, national unity is progressing in the right direction.
The Grits have never done that.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to national unity, very regrettable words were heard last Friday from a member of the C.C.F. party, about the province of Quebec. I will not go over all he said in his speech, because that would give him too much importance, but I cannot refrain from quoting a few lines that I find on page 2823 of Hansard:
One of the things that bother a great many people in Canada who do not live adjacent to among or with French Canadians is a feeling that somehow they insist in taking a different view of Canadianism and of what Canadians want and need from that of people within the rest of the country. This is a most delicate-
The hon. member does admit it.
-delicate and touchy subject for a politician to confront, but I think it needs some confronting. Like many other members who have come here in the last few years, while I have read a great deal in Canadian history about the French Canadian problem, it was not until I began to follow the French Canadian newspapers with more

The Budget-Mr. Bourbonnais
intensity that X realized the markedly different conception of Canadianism that the French Canadians have. This is something that we very much need to resolve-
He wants to change everything, solve problems that cannot be solved.
-even in the name of that magical phrase, national unity.
One feeling I have taken from reading the French Canadian press is that they have what is almost a conceit in their Canadianism. They push upon other Canadians an interpretation that X cannot accept and which I think many members of the house cannot accept. It seems that the contradistinction between their kind of Canadianism and ours is that theirs is French Canadian based upon language and Roman Catholic based upon religion and so on the other hand we have to be Protestant and English speaking. I do not think this necessarily is true.
I agree with that, Mr. Speaker.
I know that in my constituency, we have very few French Canadians. We have a good many Catholics who, in the main, are English speaking. Many of them are Italians, Poles and so on. I do not think their conception of Canadianism has to take a back seat at any time to what I might call the superiority complex of Canadianism that exists in French Canada-
This is out-and-out Maurice Lamontagne talk.

We can sense there the socialistic approach of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). He can hardly tolerate that different people should exist in Canada, people who do not wish to change their way of life, but who try to maintain their traditions, without forcing any other Canadians to copy theirs.
What the hon. member for Port Arthur means when he speaks of national unity is the great uniformity into which the great minority, or all Canadians, whatever their origin might be inmersed so as to come out good, manageable little guys who would think and speak in the same way and act all together at the bidding of a single socialist master-of an advanced Liberal, to use the phrase of a former Liberal prime minister.
However, as we have seen in the last election, Providence protected us from the scourge of the C.C.F. If the hon. member for Port Arthur thinks we are overbearing in our Canadianism, it shows how little he knows about Canadian history. Let me remind him that on the whole, French speaking Canadians are much more deeply rooted in Canadian soil than the great majority of Canadians of other languages, and that the fact that we have a different language and a different religion may perhaps appear to him as a different form of Canadianism which he will never

understand until he learns our language and lives in our province of Quebec. For a member who has pretensions to culture, his remarks show that it is very far from complete. If the hon. member thinks the French Canadians have a superiority complex, let me tell him once again that he knows nothing about history or about present conditions, despite all his titles.
What we have in the province of Quebec is a feeling of pride in many respects and for several reasons.
Incidentally, I might give some advice to the leader of the Social Democratic party, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue); we heard him when he took up the cudgels for certain South African subjects and tried to defend negroes who are oppressed in that country-no sincere Christian of course can admit that negroes, subjects of an important country, be persecuted-but he tried to force the government to interfere in the internal affairs of another country. I would ask him to look after his own household instead of interfering with what concerns other countries, and to attempt to teach his supporters that Canadianism and national unity are not based on prejudice.
I heard, last Friday, some members of the Liberal opposition protest loudly in connection with the benefits of the measure introduced by the Minister of Finance, to adjust the federal grants to universities.
If the hon. members would recall the difficult years education went through in the province of Quebec under a Liberal administration, up to 1935, they would perhaps understand why the great majority of the people of Quebec have supported the thesis of the Union Nationale and the former premier, the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, on the exclusive rights of the provinces in the field of education.
Perhaps it would be appropriate to remind them of certain statistics showing that under the former Liberal administration in the province of Quebec, education always came
last.
In 1935, the province of Quebec had 9,000 schools-I should rather say 9,000 educational institutions, since this number included all colleges and universities, special and private institutions, as well as rural schools of two or three rooms where there was only one teacher, and we had dozens of those in each parish. Now, in 1956, there were 11,000 educational institutions in the

province of Quebec, most of the small schools having been replaced by central schools of twelve to twenty classrooms.
In 1935, there were 27,000 teachers while in 1956, there were 51,900, that is 52,000. In 1935, we had 700,000 pupils in the province of Quebec, while in 1956 there were 1,116,000.
The total contribution of the taxpayers to education in the province of Quebec was $28 million in 1935; in 1956, it had reached $99 million. The provincial government's contribution to education in 1935 was $5 million and in 1956, it was $87 million.
The total amount spent on education in 1935 was $33 million, whereas in 1956, it was more than $250 million. When comparing the figures for 1935 with those of 1956, the difference between the amounts spent reflects the interest in education shown by the former Liberal government of the province in comparison with the interest shown by a Union Nationale government of Conservative trend.
Other figures show what has been done for education in the province of Quebec, because, in 1935, an amount of $1,800,000 was spent for the building and repairing of 480 schools. In 1956, 440 schools were built at a cost of $46 million. Moreover, repair work was carried out in 1,451 schools at a cost of $4,297,000 which means that in 1956, 25 times more money than in 1935 was spent for school construction and repairs. The average salary of educators in the province of Quebec varied until 1935 between $80 and $400 a year for a female teacher. No male school teacher received a salary higher than $1,500.
Today, the minimum salary of a female teacher is $1,500, and the average teachers' salary is $3,445. We therefore see the tremendous progress achieved with regard to education in the province of Quebec in the years 1935 to 1956.
This year $300 million will be spent to that end in the province of Quebec. We may therefore say that the amount spent on education in the province of Quebec will be ten times greater than in 1935. This system of assistance to education in the province of Quebec was started under a government which is known as that of the Union Nationale. That is why so many people in Quebec favour this government.
In 1952, the Liberal government tried, for political reasons, to offer assistance to universities. In Quebec, at that time, we were doubtful of the government's sincerity, recalling as we did the difficulties we had suffered
The Budget-Mr. Bourbonnais at the hands of a similar administration in the years prior to 1935. After all the money that the federal government wanted to turn over to Quebec universities had been collected from Quebec taxpayers. Why then should that money reach Quebec through Ottawa, in view of the provisions of section 93 of the British North America Act, to the effect that -and I am now going to quote that section because it has repeatedly been referred to by great politicians who always try to confuse sections 91, 92 and 93, which are nevertheless quite clear to any layman. I shall read the section in English:
(Text):
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, subject and according to the following provisions-
(Translation):
It is up to each province, then, to construe that section as it should be construed. The province of Quebec wanted to abide by that section of the constitution.
I merely wish to show that, in the province of Quebec, education is in good hands and that our province has no need of advice or help from C.C.F. pseudo-intellectuals, nor even from all those petty politicians who are more interested in their personal advancement than in that of our province and of our country.
We are proud, in the province of Quebec, of our achievements in that field in the last fifteen years. Today, if the hon. member for Port Arthur thinks that we have a superiority complex I must tell him that, when he is aware of what goes on in the province of Quebec he will understand that he is mistaken, and that it is rather a feeling of pride for us to have at last aroused the envy of our neighbours, we, who were but a poor little people exploited by blackmailers who were keeping us in ignorance in order to better exploit us and to maintain their Liberal party strong and powerful, at our expense.
In 1957, during the first session of parliament, most members voted in favour of the increase from $1 to $1.50 per capita for the purpose of assistance to universities provided by the federal government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he is anticipating, or reverting to a debate on the measure introduced by the Minister of Finance concerning grants to universities. I would ask him to drop the subject.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I only wanted to straighten out a few things.
Besides, we are discussing the budget speech, and since last week, the action taken

The Budget-Mr. Bourbonnais by the members of the province of Quebec was misunderstood, I wanted to quote certain figures and to recall certain facts.
I should like, therefore, to set out the reasons why some members from the province of Quebec voted in 1958 in favour of raising federal grants to universities.
We realized-this is my own personal view, but I think it is shared by many-we members from the province of Quebec realized that provinces other than Quebec had universities which were in great need of financial help. Those provinces were counting mostly on assistance from the federal government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order I regret having to intervene again. I thought the hon. member would limit himself to opinions of a general nature concerning certain remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), which are not necessarily related to Bill C-56, whose purpose is to amend the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
I note, however, that the hon. member is mainly working towards the point that is already covered by the bill which is to be submitted to the house and which was discussed at the resolution stage of that bill.
I would therefore ask him to drop that subject.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think that in describing the reasons which prompted us to vote, in 1958, in favour of raising the grants to universities, I am getting away from the bill.
What I wanted to say is that other provinces have universities, and that such universities have financial needs and were counting on help from the federal government.
I also had to keep in mind other provinces which did not object to federal aid to their universities. I was convinced that this government would soon find a solution that would be acceptable to the province of Quebec and that the amounts which had been reserved in trust for the universities of the province of Quebec would thereby increase and would be paid to them some day.
I wanted to show the willingness of the people of Quebec to co-operate with all the provinces of Canada and never to handicap the development of their neighbours.
What this government is now doing confirms my opinion and I am all the prouder of being a Canadian from the province of Quebec because I have an opportunity to participate, with the Conservative government, in the establishment of a Canadianism

based on the mutual respect of the various groups which form our country, and to share in measures calculated to achieve economic recovery by a wise, farsighted and sound administration.

Mr. Speaker, we have been listening for about 20 minutes to the hon. member from Vau-dreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais). Quite understandably, I do not intend to deal with his remarks at this time, for if I did so I should be out of order, just as he was.
Last Thursday, Mr. Speaker, I heard the third budget speech of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) not counting, of course, his miniature pre-election budget of 1957, as I was not yet a member of this house.
Actually, this is my third experience at getting ready to speak on the budget.
Reference to the official reports in Hansard for 1958 and 1959 will show that I was then unable to speak for lack of time. So my notes had to be filed away and unfortunately, I cannot use them this year, because they are now outdated.
I am more fortunate this year and, I think, it is an advantage to be able to make a few remarks about the budget speech of last Thursday.
May I be allowed to point out, at the beginning of my remarks, what Mr. Speaker himself said before the Ottawa branch of the alliance canadienne.
I have here a clipping of the Montreal Gazette for April 4 1960, headed:
"Mr. Michener boosts bilinguals."
This dispatch from Ottawa reads as follows: (Text):
Commons Speaker Boland Michener said that mutual understanding among English and French speaking Canadians would be reached more easily if all were bilingual.
(Translation):
The item continues, and I quote the Speaker himself:
(Text):
Each of us must strive to be a member of both groups. I look forward to a future in which we have a good knowledge of each other's languages and a perfect understanding of each other's ideals.
Coming from Mr. Speaker himself, the first member of this House of Commons, this declaration must-and I personally hope it will-do more to achieve in Canada this perfect understanding between all Canadians. I wish also to point out that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) himself paid tribute to the French speaking population of this country by delivering a part of his budget speech in my native language. He started

to speak in French and twice afterwards used the same language. For that he must be congratulated. On my part, Mr. Speaker, I want to pay tribute to the minister in speaking these few words of congratulation in his own maternal language.
(Translation):
May I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Vaudreuil-Soulanges (Mr. Bourbonnais) also had words of praise for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and it might have been the only moment in his speech where he was not out of order.
There is one thing which has always struck me-I do not say this to criticize the Minister of Finance because politicians of all parties are a bit at fault in this matter-and that is the fact that one feels the need to speak French when it comes to federal-provincial relations. That is what the Minister of Finance did, as can be seen on page 2675 of Hansard of Thursday last.
As I said, I am not blaming him for choosing that method. Should we believe that doing so will commit the government of my province to a less negative attitude towards the government of Canada? I hope so, and I also trust that the new atmosphere of agreement will continue to exist and that our province will fully benefit by its relations with Ottawa.
That friendly atmosphere, Mr. Speaker, that climate of mutual understanding might have existed under the former Liberal administration which was at the helm in this country. That government did not refer to members of the Quebec government as "those people from outside". We know the opposite is the truth. I need not emphasize what large amount of money the people of the province of Quebec lost through the negative attitude of their former premier. May I be allowed to say here that I believe that attitude was purely electoral? And I would call to witness premier Barrette, whose statements follow closely those of Mr. Sauve.
I have here a clipping from Le Devoir of March 17, 1960 reporting certain words of
The Budget-Mr. Roberge the present premier of the province when he referred to the future of Quebec universities. Let me quote part of that clipping:
Mr. Barrette made much of the talks with Ottawa-
And we do not blame him for those talks; on the contrary, we are very glad of it.
-made much of the talks with Ottawa to recuperate the accumulated grants.
And please note this:
We gave ourselves airs of independence, he added, but we were most anxious to settle the problem.
I also have a clipping from Le Devoir for March 28, 1960, or three weeks later. I shall quote only the title:

Certain things have occurred in the past.
Then there is a subtile in larger print:
Today we must go hand in hand with Ottawa.
And now here is a clipping from La Presse for Monday, March 28, 1960, which goes into greater detail on this political speech made by the premier of my province. The story starts with the same quotation:
Certain things have occurred in the past.
Farther down, the article goes on to say:
Thanks to the new climate now existing between Quebec and Ottawa, we have been able to solve problems which had been outstanding for years ... Ottawa is now treating us like friends. As long as they themselves will co-operate, I will never regret to co-operate with the central government, to give them a true hand-in-hand co-operation.
To conclude this first part of my remarks, I would add that under the former Liberal government, the door was not closed, but that it was the premier of the province of Quebec who closed it on his way out.
I do not intend to comment on those statements at this time, since we will probably have the opportunity to deal with them during the debate on the second reading of the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangement bill.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is the appropriate time to ask you to say it is now ten o'clock. (Text):

subtopic: NEW BUDWORM INSECTICIDE
NEW BUDWORM INSECTICIDE
speechtext:
1.	Is the federal government attempting to produce an insecticide that will be effective for bud-worm spraying of forests but harmless to fish?
2.	If so, what are present prospects of producing this solution?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
1.	The Department of Agriculture does not engage directly in the production of new chemical insecticides. This is done by chemical corporations, who are devoting very considerable effort toward the production of selective chemicals which are poisonous to one form of life but not to others.
Fundamental research by the department in this field is devoted primarily to the study of physiology and the mode of action of chemical insecticides to develop the basic knowledge necessary to the production of selective chemicals.
2.	In view of the many problems inherent in developing a suitable highly efficient poison for one form of life, but which will have no effect on other forms of life, it is not possible to predict when such a chemical will be available for budworm control.
The department is taking a leading role in the development and testing of insecticidal toxins, which are products of insect disease organisms, and which have no ill effects on forms of life other than insects. Field trials of these against the spruce budworm and other related pests are being planned for 1960.
